The library itself will stay open on its usual schedule. The entrance on the playground side is the west entrance, and it will be open as normal. The east entrance has to close because the direct path from the bus shelter to it will be behind a temporary barrier. You can still wait at the bus shelter.

**Coming from the playground:** use the west entrance as usual.

**Coming from the bus shelter:** follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This adds about 120 metres to your journey. The path has no steps, but one section has a temporary firm mat laid over uneven ground. The east entrance is closed to everyone during the work, including wheelchair users, and the mat is on the route to the west entrance.

**If you would like help:** library staff can meet you at the bus shelter and walk with you to the west entrance. Please call the library desk before you set out to ask for this. You can also ask when you arrive, using the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be free straight away. This help is available only during library opening hours. We cannot provide transport around the building.

**Returning books:** the returns slot beside the east entrance cannot be used during the closure. Any book due from Monday through Thursday, including books borrowed from another branch, can be returned on Friday without a late charge.

**If the work runs late:** heavy rain may make the work take longer. If it does, we will post an updated notice at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will stay in place unless that notice announces a further extension.

Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed matches the number on your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure, and ask a steward before planting in a bed whose number you cannot read. The narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively; it is not an unclaimed bed.

Tools with blue handles are shared. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without blue handles may belong to another gardener, so do not assume they are shared. You will find the shed code on your membership card. Please close the door when you leave to keep rain off the lower shelves.

The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees, but not individual beds—even those belonging to gardeners on the rota. If you will be away, you can arrange separately for another gardener to water your bed. Only add the arrangement to the noticeboard with their agreement, so a request does not look like a job they have already accepted.

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads in the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a sorting precaution, not a judgment about anyone’s gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. Check the noticeboard for the next session and any cancellation. We are glad you are here, and we would much rather answer a small question before planting than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else’s bed.

Tools without a blue handle may belong to another gardener, so don't assume they're free to use. The shed code is on your membership card. Please close the door behind you, since rain gets to the lower shelves when the door is left open.

If you'll be away, you can arrange cover with another gardener. Please add that arrangement to the noticeboard only once the other gardener has agreed, so that a request doesn't look like a job someone has already taken on.

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Weeds with seed heads belong in the covered brown bin. If you're not sure whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a precaution, not a judgment on anyone's gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. The noticeboard shows the next session and any cancellations. We're glad you're here, and we'd much rather answer a small question before you plant than help move a thriving crop out of someone else's bed.

The proposed worksheet imports blank readings from the instrument log, replacing the current worksheet’s requirement that an operator enter a blank separately for each sample. The comparison evaluated agreement between the resulting background-corrected fluorescence values and the time required to produce them. It did not assess accuracy relative to a known true concentration; no certified reference material was included.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings; each aliquot was measured only once. The manual worksheet was completed before the imported worksheet was generated, so the operator could not see the imported results during manual entry. Aliquots were measured in a fixed order by solution number. Although each solution contributed multiple aliquots, the worksheet comparison contained no independent repeat measurements of the instrument signal.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed at the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. All three differences occurred in the final solution, where a single blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log, making the manual corrected values 0.2 units lower. After the initial comparison, replacing the copied entry with the logged blank eliminated the displayed differences for all 24 aliquots. This post-comparison correction is distinct from the initial result.

The initial discrepancies are consistent with a single transcription error propagated across three rows, rather than three independent transcription errors. Because only one operator participated and knew that the comparison concerned data entry, the result does not estimate a routine operator error rate. Agreement after correction supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement beyond the displayed precision, accuracy relative to true concentration, or correct blank assignment in future instrument logs.

Producing the imported worksheet took four minutes, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking—a seven-minute reduction in this session. These timings excluded instrument operation and the subsequent discrepancy investigation. The observed time saving applies to this session and its particular number of rows; its persistence when log formats change or missing blanks require operator intervention was not evaluated.

## Background Subtraction: Manual Versus Imported Blank Values

### Purpose

In this fluorescence workflow, the current worksheet requires an operator to enter the blank reading by hand for each sample. We compared it with a proposed worksheet that imports the blank reading from the instrument log. The aim was to reduce transcription errors. Removing manual entry might also change agreement between the two methods, but this comparison measures agreement between corrected values only. It does not assess either worksheet against a known true concentration, and no certified reference material was included.

### Design

Twenty-four aliquots were prepared from eight solutions, with three aliquots per solution, and all were measured in one session. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings. Each aliquot was measured once, so the comparison contains no independent repeats of the instrument signal, even though it contains more than one aliquot per prepared solution.

Measurement order was fixed by solution number. The manual worksheet was completed before the imported worksheet was generated, and the operator could not see the imported results while entering manual values.

### Initial Comparison

Corrected values agreed to the instrument's displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. All three remaining differences occurred in the final solution. One blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. The saved instrument log showed that the copied entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows. The manual corrected values were therefore 0.2 units lower than the imported values.

### Correction

After the initial comparison, the copied entry was replaced with the logged blank. With this change, the corrected values agreed for all 24 aliquots at displayed precision. This correction was made after the initial comparison and is reported separately from it. The 24-of-24 agreement therefore describes the corrected manual worksheet, not the original entries.

### Interpretation

The initial differences are consistent with a transcription mechanism in this session. They should not be read as an estimate of a routine operator error rate. Only one operator used the worksheet, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry. The three affected aliquots also do not represent three independent transcription errors, because they trace to a single copied entry.

The absence of displayed differences after correction is useful evidence that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement at greater precision, and it does not show that blank assignment will be correct in future instrument logs.

### Timing

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, and manual entry and checking took eleven minutes. These times exclude instrument operation and the later investigation of the discrepancy, and they reflect this session's number of rows. We have not measured whether the time saving persists when log formats change or when an operator must resolve a missing blank.

# Spoken Location Cue After Closing a Note: Research Summary

## Question

Does a spoken cue that announces the current row label help screen-reader users return to a table after they close a note? And if it does, what does the cue cost?

## Prototype and Design

We compared two versions:

- **Cue version:** When a note closes, the current row label is spoken.
- **Existing version:** Keyboard focus returns to the same cell, with no added cue.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The two sets of tasks used different tables. For half of each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside the timed interval.

## Timing Results

- Median of participant-level mean completion times: **38 seconds** with the cue, **41 seconds** without it.
- This compares two medians of participant means. It is not the median of twelve within-person differences.
- Seven participants had a lower personal mean with the cue. Three had a higher mean. Two were equal at the recorded precision.
- We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test.

So the timing data points in one direction, but it does not establish a reliable difference. Seven of twelve is a split, not a pattern we can call settled.

## Orientation Feedback

In the closing interview, nine of twelve participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described moments when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to.

The other three reported no orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype.

Two points to keep apart:

- Not asking for removal is not the same as wanting the cue on by default. Participants were not asked to choose a default, so we have no data on that.
- This is exploratory interview feedback. It is not a measured performance result.

## Limitations

- **Order effects:** Counterbalancing removed the complete alignment of version and practice, but not every learning effect. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first set of tasks that carried into the second.
- **Participants:** Less experienced users were not recruited. We don't know how they would respond.
- **Table size:** The tables fit on one screen in the prototype. The study says nothing about performance on large tables.

## Interpretation

The orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. The interruption reports show that added speech can compete with speech the user is already hearing. That competition is a design question regardless of whether the timing difference proves reliable.

## Next Steps

A next version could make the cue interruptible, so it yields to ongoing speech. We did not implement or test that behavior. The timings in this study should not be cited as evidence that an interruptible cue performs better.

Open questions for the next round:

- Does the timing difference hold with more participants and a confidence interval?
- How do less experienced users respond?
- Does the effect hold on tables larger than one screen?
- Do users prefer the cue on by default when asked directly?

# Spoken row cue after closing a note: research summary

## The question

Does a spoken location cue help screen-reader users return to a table after opening a note? We built a version that speaks the current row label when the note closes. The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same cell and adds no cue.

## What we did

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six started with the cue version and six with the existing version. The two sets of tasks used different tables, and for half of each order group we reversed which tables went with which version.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval.

## What we found

**Time.** The median of the twelve participant-level mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. That is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two were equal at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so we can't say whether the three-second gap is reliable.

**Interviews.** Nine participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described times when the cue cut across speech they were still listening to. The other three reported no orientation benefit. None of the twelve asked us to remove the feature.

That last point is easy to over-read. Not asking for removal is not the same as wanting the cue on by default, and we never asked participants to choose a default. The interview comments are self-reported impressions, not measured performance.

## What this supports

An orientation benefit looks plausible for some users on these tasks. The timing direction is consistent with that, but it is weak evidence on its own.

The study also shows that added speech can compete with speech the user is still hearing. That is a design problem whether or not a time difference eventually proves reliable. A faster cue that talks over the user is not an obvious win.

## What this does not support

- **Learning effects.** Our counterbalancing broke the complete alignment between version and practice, but it did not remove every possible learning effect. A search strategy picked up in the first set of tasks may have carried into the second.
- **Less experienced users.** We did not recruit them, so we don't know how they would respond.
- **Large tables.** The prototype tables were short enough to fit on one screen. We have no performance evidence for large tables, which is where a location cue might matter most.
- **Default behavior.** The data say nothing about whether the cue should ship enabled.

## What to do next

An interruptible cue is a reasonable next version. We did not implement or test it here, so the current timings are not evidence for it and should not be presented that way.

The next test should follow the user's attention, not just the clock. Does the cue arrive while the user is still listening to something else? Does the user act on it or talk past it? The same study should include less experienced users and tables longer than one screen, and should ask participants directly about defaults. If we want a claim about speed, we also need the interval estimate and test we haven't yet run.

response:
The growing waiting list calls for action, but we should distinguish between opening places and deciding how much disruption that requires. There are twenty full beds and ten households waiting. Dividing every returning gardener’s bed in half may seem a fair starting point: nobody wants access to depend on having been lucky enough to join years ago. Yet we are allocating more than land. We are also allocating the chance to keep crops through their growing cycles. For that reason, I support dividing vacant beds first and allowing returning gardeners to keep their present beds for one more season.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds, allowing eight offers to households on the waiting list. Assuming every offer is accepted, two households would remain without a bed. That is a real cost, and we should not describe the proposal as clearing the list. It would nevertheless open places for most waiting households without requiring every returning gardener to disrupt established planting at once.

Protecting established planting deserves scrutiny, because it can also protect an established advantage. A perennial cannot give its gardener a permanent claim to shared land. Our membership agreement promises a bed for a season, with renewal decided annually. The justification for one more season in an existing bed is therefore a limited transition, not an entitlement to continued possession. The committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open, so that this temporary arrangement does not become a permanent rule by default.

That published rule must cover new members as well as returning ones. A household accepting a half bed also needs notice of any future decision to merge, move, or resize it. Otherwise, we risk recreating the uncertainty we are trying to reduce. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size. I would like the next set of fraction worksheets to include one worked example followed by a problem that asks pupils to explain a different method. At present, every example ends with a sequence of steps, and every practice problem asks pupils to repeat it. This is efficient when the immediate aim is to practise the sequence. I am less sure that successful repetition tells us whether pupils understand why it applies.

Last week’s lesson brought that distinction into focus. After copying an example involving equal denominators, several pupils added the numerators and denominators separately on a later question. I had not collected a starting question, so I do not know how many already held that misunderstanding. Nor can I say that the worked example caused it; the lesson may simply have exposed it. What I can say is that correct copying on the first practice question did not prevent the misunderstanding from appearing on the next.

The explanation problem I propose would show two correct solutions to the same addition: one using equivalent fractions and one using a diagram. Pupils would explain where the same quantity appears in both solutions. The aim would be to make their understanding more visible, rather than to ask which method is always better. A diagram may illuminate these numbers but become cumbersome with others. I would not want a useful representation to become another compulsory routine.

Making room for this would cost space and lesson time. I would replace one existing repetition question, rather than add a page. Pupils who need more practice with the original sequence could use the spare practice sheet we already have. That seems a practical arrangement, though it is not evidence that one explanation problem will meet everyone’s needs.

We could try the revised sheet in one lesson and collect pupils’ explanations before deciding whether to keep it. This would help us see what the responses reveal about pupils’ understanding and whether teachers find the sheet workable. Without a comparison planned in advance, it would not establish that the change improves attainment. I think those more limited questions still give us enough reason to try a bounded change.

**Theorem.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and set
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then each \(d_n\ge0\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) once \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Because the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, consider its first \(N\) terms. The intermediate terms cancel:
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})
=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Since \(a_n\to0\), this difference becomes smaller than any positive number for all sufficiently large \(N\). Therefore the partial sums \(S_N\) tend to \(a_1\). By definition, this means that the series converges and has sum \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]
The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is exactly \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\). Hence the infinite tail exists and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to0\) provides an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), we therefore have
\[
0\le \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease is needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n=0\), and the same identities still hold. \(\square\)

\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge0\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an \(N\ge1\) for which this tail is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, we first add its first \(N\) terms. Substituting the definition of \(d_n\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The intermediate terms cancel: each of \(a_2,\ldots,a_N\) appears once with each sign. Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to0\), this difference tends to zero. Hence the partial sums \(S_N\) tend to \(a_1\), which is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular,
\[
\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n-a_{N+1}\right|=a_{M+1}.
\]
As \(M\to\infty\), the right-hand side tends to zero. The finite sums of the tail therefore converge to \(a_{N+1}\), proving
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to0\) provides an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). Taking \(N=K\), we obtain
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The argument also includes zero terms and equal consecutive terms: neither cancellation nor the limit calculation requires strict decrease. \(\square\)

# Telescoping Series and Tails

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Put
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \qquad (n \ge 1).$$
Then:

1. every $d_n$ is nonnegative;
2. the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$;
3. for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$;
4. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an integer $N \ge 1$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

---

## Proof

Throughout, recall what it means for a series to converge: a series $\sum_{n=p}^\infty c_n$ converges to $S$ when its partial sums $\sum_{n=p}^{M} c_n$ approach $S$ as $M \to \infty$. We will check this directly from the definition, using only limits of sequences.

**Step 1: Each $d_n$ is nonnegative.**
Since $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$. Subtracting gives $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

**Step 2: Write the partial sums as telescoping sums.**
Fix integers $M > N \ge 1$. We compute two finite sums. In each one, the terms cancel in pairs from the inside, so only the first and last endpoints survive.

For the first $N$ terms:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) = a_1 - a_{N+1}. \tag{1}$$
Here $-a_2$ from the first bracket cancels $+a_2$ from the second, and so on, leaving $a_1$ and $-a_{N+1}$.

For the terms from $N+1$ to $M$:
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}$$
The same cancellation happens here, leaving $a_{N+1}$ and $-a_{M+1}$.

Identity (1) is the one with a fixed upper limit $N$. Identity (2) is the tail, with a fixed starting point $N+1$ and an upper limit $M$ that will grow.

**Step 3: The series converges to $a_1$.**
Let $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n$ be the partial sums of the series. By (1),
$$S_N = a_1 - a_{N+1}.$$
Since $a_n \to 0$, we have $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. Therefore $S_N \to a_1$. By definition, the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges and its sum is $a_1$.

**Step 4: The tail equals $a_{N+1}$.**
Fix $N \ge 1$. The partial sums of the tail are given by (2):
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.$$
As $M \to \infty$, we have $a_{M+1} \to 0$, because $M+1 \to \infty$ and $a_n \to 0$. The value $a_{N+1}$ does not depend on $M$, so the partial sums converge to $a_{N+1}$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}.$$
This is the tail identity in the theorem.

**Step 5: The tail can be made small.**

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Put $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$. In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Nonnegativity.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$, so $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

*Partial sums.* Fix integers $M > N \ge 1$. We compute two finite sums by telescoping. In each sum, the terms $-a_{k+1}$ from one summand cancel the terms $a_{k+1}$ from the next, so only the first and last terms survive.

For the first $N$ terms,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the terms from $N+1$ through $M$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

*Limits.* Let $M \to \infty$ in the first identity, which does not involve $M$, to get the partial sums of the whole series. Since $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, the partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = a_1 - a_{N+1}$ converge to $a_1$. So the series converges, with sum $a_1$.

For the tail, fix $N$ and let $M \to \infty$ in the second identity. Since $a_{M+1} \to 0$, we get

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$

This is the claimed tail formula. It holds for every $N \ge 1$.

*Tail bound.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $a_k \to 0$, there is an index $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. Set $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N + 1 \ge K$, so

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

*Edge cases.* If $a_1 = 0$, then nonnegativity and monotonicity force $a_n = 0$ for all $n$, since $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$. The identities above still hold, with every term equal to zero. If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The argument never needed a strict decrease, only $a_{n+1} \le a_n$.

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Define
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \qquad (n \ge 1).
$$
Then $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n$. The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges to $a_1$. For every integer $N \ge 1$,
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$
In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ for which this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

**Step 1: The terms are nonnegative.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$. Therefore
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0.
$$

**Step 2: The partial sums telescope.** A series converges to $S$ when its partial sums converge to $S$, so we compute the partial sums directly. For each integer $M \ge 1$,
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{M} d_n = \sum_{n=1}^{M} \bigl(a_n - a_{n+1}\bigr) = a_1 - a_{M+1}. \tag{1}
$$
To see why, look at the terms that appear. For each $k$ with $2 \le k \le M$, the term $a_k$ appears twice: with a plus sign in $d_k$ and with a minus sign in $d_{k-1}$. These cancel. The only terms that do not cancel are $a_1$ (from $d_1$, with a plus sign) and $-a_{M+1}$ (from $d_M$, with a minus sign). This gives (1).

Now let $M > N \ge 1$. Subtracting the partial sum up to $N$ from the partial sum up to $M$ gives the sum of the terms between them:
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
= \sum_{n=1}^{M} d_n - \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
= (a_1 - a_{M+1}) - (a_1 - a_{N+1})
= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}
$$

**Step 3: The series converges to $a_1$.** Because $a_n \to 0$, we have $a_{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$. By (1),
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{M} d_n = \lim_{M\to\infty} \bigl(a_1 - a_{M+1}\bigr) = a_1 - 0 = a_1.
$$
So the series converges, and its sum is $a_1$. This uses only the explicit formula (1) and the definition of the limit of a sequence. No convergence theorem for series is needed.

**Step 4: The tail equals $a_{N+1}$.** Fix an integer $N \ge 1$. The tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ is the limit of the partial sums in (2) as $M \to \infty$:
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = \lim_{M\to\infty} \bigl(a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}\bigr) = a_{N+1} - 0 = a_{N+1}.
$$
This agrees with Step 3. The full sum $a_1$ minus the first $N$ terms, $a_1 - (a_1 - a_{N+1})$, is also $a_{N+1}$.

**Step 5: The tail can be made small.** Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $a_k \to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. Put
$$
N = \max(1, K).
$$
Then $N + 1 \ge K$, so Step 4 gives
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

**Remarks.**

- If $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for every $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is zero. Identities (1) and (2) still hold, and the sum is $0 = a_1$. No separate argument is needed.
- If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The argument uses only $d_n \ge 0$ and the identities (1) and (2). It does not require the sequence to decrease strictly.

# Telescoping Series and Their Tails

## Theorem

Let (aₙ), n ≥ 1, be a sequence of real numbers such that

* aₙ ≥ 0 for all n (nonnegative),
* aₙ ≥ aₙ₊₁ for all n (nonincreasing),
* aₙ → 0 as n → ∞.

Define dₙ = aₙ − aₙ₊₁. Then:

1. dₙ ≥ 0 for every n.
2. The series Σₙ₌₁^∞ dₙ converges, and its sum is a₁.
3. For every integer N ≥ 1, the tail Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^∞ dₙ converges and equals aₙ₊₁.
4. For every ε > 0 there is an N such that this tail is less than ε.

## Definitions used

A series Σ cₙ **converges to S** if its partial sums, the finite sums c_p + c_{p+1} + … + c_M, approach S as M → ∞. This is all we need. No convergence theorem is cited.

The statement aₙ → 0 means: for every ε > 0 there is a K such that aₖ < ε for all k ≥ K. (Because aₖ ≥ 0, this is the same as |aₖ| < ε.)

## Proof

**Step 1: dₙ ≥ 0.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, aₙ ≥ aₙ₊₁, so dₙ = aₙ − aₙ₊₁ ≥ 0. If two consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding dₙ is simply 0. We never need a strict decrease.

**Step 2: Finite sums collapse.** Fix integers M > N ≥ 1. Write out the sum of the first N differences:

Σₙ₌₁^N dₙ = (a₁ − a₂) + (a₂ − a₃) + … + (a_N − a_{N+1}).

Each term −aₖ (for 2 ≤ k ≤ N) cancels against the +aₖ in the next bracket. Only the very first and very last entries survive:

**(A)** Σₙ₌₁^N dₙ = a₁ − a_{N+1}.

The same cancellation applies to the differences from N+1 to M:

Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^M dₙ = (a_{N+1} − a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} − a_{N+3}) + … + (a_M − a_{M+1}),

and only a_{N+1} and −a_{M+1} survive:

**(B)** Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^M dₙ = a_{N+1} − a_{M+1}.

**Step 3: The full series converges to a₁.** By (A), the Mth partial sum of Σ dₙ is a₁ − a_{M+1}. Let ε > 0. Since aₙ → 0, there is a K with a_k < ε for all k ≥ K. Then for every M ≥ K,

|(a₁ − a_{M+1}) − a₁| = a_{M+1} < ε.

So the partial sums approach a₁, which means Σₙ₌₁^∞ dₙ = a₁.

**Step 4: The tail equals a_{N+1}.** Fix N ≥ 1. By (B), the partial sums of the tail series Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^∞ dₙ are a_{N+1} − a_{M+1}, for M > N. Here a_{N+1} is a fixed number and only a_{M+1} changes with M. Given ε > 0, choose K as before. For every M ≥ K,

|(a_{N+1} − a_{M+1}) − a_{N+1}| = a_{M+1} < ε.

So these partial sums approach a_{N+1}, which means Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^∞ dₙ = a_{N+1}.

As a consistency check, this agrees with Step 3. The total a₁ minus the first N terms a₁ − a_{N+1} leaves a_{N+1}.

**Step 5: The tail can be made small.** Let ε > 0. Choose K such that aₖ < ε whenever k ≥ K, and take N = max(1, K). Then N + 1 > K, so by Step 4

Σₙ₌ₙ₊₁^∞ dₙ = a_{N+1} < ε. ∎

## Remarks

* **The case a₁ = 0.** Then 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ a₁ = 0 for all n, so every aₙ and every dₙ is 0. The argument above needs no change: both sides of every identity are 0.
* **Where each hypothesis was used.** Nonincreasing gives dₙ ≥ 0 (Step 1). The limit aₙ → 0 makes the leftover term a_{M+1} vanish (Steps 3 and 4). Nonnegativity lets us drop absolute values when applying the limit. Telescoping, the cancellation in (A) and (B), is what makes the partial sums computable exactly.

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $a_n\to 0$, and put $d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}$. Then:

1. $d_n\ge 0$ for every $n$.
2. The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$.
3. For every integer $N\ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.
4. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: the terms are nonnegative.* Since $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$, so
$$
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}\ge 0 .
$$
If $a_n=a_{n+1}$ then $d_n=0$. The argument below never needs a strict decrease.

*Step 2: finite sums telescope.* Fix integers $M>N\ge 1$. Writing out the sum of the first $N$ terms, each $a_k$ with $2\le k\le N$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so these cancel in pairs:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$
The same cancellation applies to the terms from $N+1$ through $M$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+(a_{N+2}-a_{N+3})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

*Step 3: the series converges to $a_1$.* By definition, the series converges to a number $S$ when its partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n$ tend to $S$ as $N\to\infty$. By (1) the partial sums are $a_1-a_{N+1}$. Because $a_{N+1}\to 0$, we get
$$
\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n=\lim_{N\to\infty}\bigl(a_1-a_{N+1}\bigr)=a_1 .
$$
So $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n=a_1$.

*Step 4: the tail equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix $N\ge 1$. The tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ is the limit, as $M\to\infty$, of the sums $\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n$. By (2), these sums equal $a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}$. Here $a_{N+1}$ is a fixed number and $a_{M+1}\to 0$, so
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty}\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n=\lim_{M\to\infty}\bigl(a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}\bigr)=a_{N+1}.
$$
Hence the tail converges and
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n=a_{N+1}.
$$
This agrees with Step 3 and (1), since $a_1-\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n=a_{N+1}$.

*Step 5: the tail can be made small.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $a_k\to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Take $N=\max(1,K)$. Then $N+1>K$, so by Step 4
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon .
$$

*Remark.* If $a_1=0$, then $0\le a_n\le a_1=0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is zero. The identities above still hold in this case. $\blacksquare$

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $a_n \to 0$. Put $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then

1. $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n$,
2. the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges and its sum is $a_1$,
3. for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.

In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that the tail after $N$ terms is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: each $d_n$ is nonnegative.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$, so
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0 .
$$

*Step 2: two finite sums.* Each $d_n$ is a difference of consecutive terms, so in a finite sum all but two terms cancel. For $N \ge 1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$
Here each $a_k$ with $2 \le k \le N$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. In the same way, for integers $M > N \ge 1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

*Step 3: the series converges to $a_1$.* A series converges to a number $s$ when its partial sums converge to $s$. By (1), the $N$th partial sum is $a_1 - a_{N+1}$. Since $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$,
$$
\lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = \lim_{N\to\infty} \bigl(a_1 - a_{N+1}\bigr) = a_1 .
$$
So $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges and equals $a_1$. No convergence test is needed, because the partial sums are given explicitly.

*Step 4: the tail equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix $N \ge 1$. The tail is the series $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$, whose partial sums are the sums in (2) as $M$ increases. Since $a_{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$ and $N$ is fixed,
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty} \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = \lim_{M\to\infty} \bigl(a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}\bigr) = a_{N+1} .
$$
So the tail converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.

*Step 5: the tail can be made small.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Because $a_k \to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that
$$
a_k < \varepsilon \quad\text{for all } k \ge K .
$$
Take $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N + 1 > K$, so by Step 4
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon .
$$
This proves the claim. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

- If $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is zero. The identities above still hold, with both sides equal to $0$.
- If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The proof never uses a strict decrease, so repeated terms cause no difficulty.

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives \(1\), since \(\binom n0=1\).

Now assume \(k\ge1\). We count **marked selections**: valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) marked selections.

We can also construct them by choosing a start and recording the gaps between selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start label. Beginning there and moving clockwise, number the selected plots \(1,\ldots,k\). Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with the last gap returning to the start. For \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The no-neighbor condition says that every gap is positive, including the last one. Since exactly \(n-k\) plots are unselected,
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,\qquad g_i\ge1.
\]
To count these ordered gap lists, arrange \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and every allowed gap list determines exactly those separators. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap lists. When \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the one possible gap list.

A start label and a gap list uniquely determine a marked selection: select the start, then move clockwise, leaving the prescribed number of unselected plots before each next selected plot. The gaps and selected plots together occupy
\[
(n-k)+k=n
\]
plots, so the final gap returns exactly to the start. Positivity of every gap ensures that no selected plots are neighbors. Conversely, every marked selection gives exactly one start label and one gap list.

Therefore,
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly \(k\) times, once for each possible mark, and \(k>0\). Hence
\[
A(n,k)=\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Using the factorial definition of the binomial coefficients,
\[
\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n(n-k-1)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
Here \(n-2k\ge0\) and \(n-k>0\), so all expressions are defined.

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is \(1\), which is allowed. Throughout, the labels remain fixed: we remove only the choice of mark, and do not identify selections under rotation. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also count these marked selections by describing the gaps between selected plots. Choose the starting plot in \(n\) ways, then list the selected plots clockwise from that start. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot. The last gap returns to the start, so it includes the circular boundary. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

No two selected plots are neighbors precisely when every gap is positive. Since every unselected plot belongs to exactly one gap, we need
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, put \(n-k\) objects in a row. There are \(n-k-1\) internal spaces between consecutive objects. Choosing \(k-1\) of those spaces for separators splits the row into \(k\) nonempty blocks, whose lengths give \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each such tuple determines exactly those separator positions. Thus the number of tuples is
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain one block, as required.

A starting plot and a gap tuple determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise, leaving \(g_i\) plots unselected before reaching the next selected plot. The \(k\) selected plots and the \(n-k\) unselected plots account for exactly one circuit of the circle. Conversely, a marked selection determines its start and all its gaps. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection has been counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) selected plots. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap must be one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have fixed, distinct labels, and selections using different labels are different selections. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also construct a marked selection by choosing its start and specifying the gaps between its selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start. Beginning there, number the selected plots in clockwise order. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with the last gap returning to the start. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The condition that selected plots are not neighbors means that every gap is positive. Every unselected plot belongs to exactly one gap, so
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, put \(n-k\) objects in a row and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The separators divide the row into \(k\) nonempty groups, whose sizes are \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each such tuple specifies exactly where the separators go. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators, giving the single tuple \((n-1)\).

A chosen start and gap tuple determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise from the start, leaving \(g_1\) plots unselected before the next selected plot, and continue in this way. The selected plots and gaps occupy
\[
k+(g_1+\cdots+g_k)=n
\]
plots, so the final gap returns exactly to the start. Because every gap is positive, the selection is valid, including across the circular boundary. Conversely, a marked selection determines its start and all its gaps. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) possible marks, and \(k>0\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

When \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have distinct fixed labels, and we are counting selections of those labeled plots. \(\square\)

response:
# Revised Proof: Non-Adjacent Selections on a Labeled Circle

**Setting.** Label the plots $1,\dots,n$ clockwise around a circle, with $n\ge 3$. Plot $i$ is adjacent to $i+1$, indices taken mod $n$, so plot $n$ is adjacent to plot $1$. For $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that no two plots of $S$ are adjacent, including the pair $\{n,1\}$. We prove

$$A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\,\binom{n-k}{k}.$$

Since $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, we have $n-k\ge k\ge 0$ and $n-k\ge 1$, so the denominator is nonzero and the binomial coefficient is an ordinary one.

---

**Case $k=0$ (empty selection).** The only $0$-element subset is $\varnothing$. It contains no pair of plots, so it is valid, and $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1\cdot 1=1$. The two agree.

**Case $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.** The rest of the proof assumes $k\ge 1$.

**Step 1: Count marked selections two ways.** Let
$$P=\{(S,s): S \text{ is a valid } k\text{-selection},\ s\in S\}.$$
Here $s$ is a "start," a chosen selected plot.

- *By selection:* each valid $S$ has exactly $k$ choices of $s$. So $|P|=k\,A(n,k)$.
- *By start:* we count $P$ differently in Steps 2–4.

The division by $k$ is legitimate because each valid $S$ contributes exactly $k$ pairs to $P$. The fibers of the projection $(S,s)\mapsto S$ all have size $k\ge 1$, so $A(n,k)=|P|/k$ exactly.

**Step 2: Encode a pair by its gap sequence.** Fix $(S,s)\in P$. Starting at $s$ and moving clockwise, list the selected plots as $p_1=s,p_2,\dots,p_k$ in clockwise order. For $i=1,\dots,k$, let $p_{k+1}=p_1$, and define

$$g_i=\text{the number of unselected plots strictly between } p_i \text{ and } p_{i+1} \text{ going clockwise.}$$

When $k=1$, $p_2=p_1$ and $g_1$ counts all $n-1$ other plots, which are all unselected.

The gaps have two properties:

- **(a) Each $g_i\ge 1$.** The plots $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are distinct selected plots, so they are not adjacent. Hence at least one plot lies strictly between them clockwise. For $k=1$, $g_1=n-1\ge 2$ because $n\ge 3$.
- **(b) $\sum_i g_i=n-k$.** The $k$ gaps are disjoint and together contain every unselected plot exactly once.

Let $G$ be the set of ordered $k$-tuples $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Step 2 defines a map $(S,s)\mapsto(s,g)$ from $P$ to $[n]\times G$.

**Step 3: This map is a bijection.** Define $\Phi:[n]\times G\to P$ as follows. Given $s$ and $g=(g_1,\dots,g_k)\in G$, set the clockwise offsets
$$d_1=0,\qquad d_{i+1}=d_i+(g_i+1)\quad (i=1,\dots,k-1),$$
and let $p_i=s+d_i \pmod n$, with $S=\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$.

*Well-defined.* Since each $g_i+1\ge 2$, the offsets are strictly increasing. Also $d_k=\sum_{i<k}(g_i+1)=(n-k)+k-(g_k+1)=n-(g_k+1)<n$, so the offsets $d_1,\dots,d_k$ lie in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and are distinct. Thus the $p_i$ are $k$ distinct plots, and $s=p_1\in S$.

*Valid.* Take two distinct selected plots $a,b$. The clockwise distance from $a$ to $b$ is a sum of one or more terms $g_j+1\ge 2$, and the same holds for the clockwise distance from $b$ to $a$. Neither distance equals $1$, so $a$ and $b$ are not adjacent. This covers the wraparound pair as well.

*Inverse.* Given $(S,s)\in P$, the gap sequence of Step 2 satisfies $d_i=$ clockwise distance from $s$ to $p_i$, and $\Phi$ rebuilds exactly $S$ from it. Conversely, $\Phi(s,g)$ has start $s$ and gap sequence $g$, because its offsets are exactly the $d_i$ above. So $\Phi$ and the Step 2 map are mutually inverse.

Therefore $|P|=n\,|G|$. The factor $n$ is the number of possible start labels.

**Step 4: Count $G$.** Put $m=n-k$. Map a tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)\in G$ to the cut set $\{c_1,\dots,c_{k-1}\}$, where $c_j=g_1+\cdots+g_j$. Since every $g_j\ge 1$, we have $0<c_1<\cdots<c_{k-1}<m$, so this is a $(k-1)$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m-1\}$. The inverse takes $g_j=c_j-c_{j-1}$ with $c_0=0$ and $c_k=m$, which gives positive parts summing to $m$. So
$$|G|=\binom{m-1}{k-1}=\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$
This is the stars-and-bars count: a row of $m$ unselected plots has $m-1$ internal gaps, and $k-1$ of them are cut.

**Step 5: Combine.** From Steps 1, 3, and 4,
$$k\,A(n,k)=|P|=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},\qquad\text{so}\qquad A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.$$

**Step 6: Convert to the stated form.** Since $n-k\ge k\ge1$, the binomial coefficients are defined. Using factorials,
$$\binom{n-k}{k}=\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},\qquad \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}=\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}.$$
The ratio is
$$\frac{\binom{n-k}{k}}{\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}}=\frac{(n-k)!}{(n-k-1)!}\cdot\frac{(k-1)!}{k!}=\frac{n-k}{k},$$
so $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}=\frac{k}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$. Substituting into Step 5,
$$A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{k}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.\qquad\blacksquare$$

---

**Remarks and checks.**

- **Why no rotation quotient.** $A(n,k)$ counts subsets of *labeled* plots, so distinct rotations of a configuration are distinct subsets and are counted separately. The only division in the proof is the division by $k$ in Step 1, which is justified by the exact fiber size.
- **Boundary case $k=n/2$ ($n$ even).** Here $n-k=k$, so the only composition is $(1,\dots,1)$ and $|G|=1$. The formula gives $A=n/k=2$. This matches the two diagonal selections $\{1,3\},\{2,4\}$ when $n=4$.
- **Example $n=5$, $k=2$.** Here $m=3$ and $G=\{(1,2),(2,1)\}$, so $|P|=5\cdot 2=10$ and $A=10/2=5$. The formula gives $\frac{5}{3}\binom{3}{2}=5$. The five valid pairs are $\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,4\},\{2,5\},\{3,5\}$.
- **Range of $k$.** The restriction $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is used in Step 6 to keep $n-k\ge k$. For larger $k$ the count is $0$, and the displayed formula should not be applied there without checking.

**Claim.** Let $n \ge 3$ labeled plots be arranged in a circle, and let $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of plots that contain no two neighboring plots, where plot $n$ and plot $1$ count as neighbors. Then
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only selection is the empty set, which has no selected plot. So $A(n,0)=1$. The right-hand side is $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$, so the formula holds. The empty selection has no plot that can be marked as a start, so it cannot enter the counting below and must be handled separately.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $P$ be the set of pairs $(S,p)$, where $S$ is a valid $k$-selection and $p \in S$ is a marked selected plot. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of marked plot, so
$$
|P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count $P$ in a second way. Fix the label $p$ of the marked plot. Since the plots have distinct labels, the $n$ possible values of $p$ give disjoint sets of pairs, so $|P|$ is the sum over these $n$ values.

For a fixed $p$, walk clockwise from $p$ and list the selected plots in order as $x_1=p, x_2, \dots, x_k$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $x_i$ and the next selected plot, where $x_{k+1}$ means $x_1=p$ again. When $k=1$, $g_1$ counts the $n-1$ unselected plots between $p$ and itself going around the circle, so $g_1=n-1$.

Two facts about the gaps follow.

- Each $g_i \ge 1$, because no two neighboring plots are both selected.
- $g_1+\dots+g_k = n-k$, because the $k$ selected plots and the $g_i$ unselected plots together make up all $n$ plots.

**The map is a bijection.** Send $(S,p)$ to the pair consisting of $p$ and the gap tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Conversely, given $p$ and a tuple of positive integers $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ summing to $n-k$, start at $p$, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise, mark the next plot as $x_2$, skip $g_2$ plots, and continue. After $k$ such steps the walk has covered $n$ plots and returns to $p$. The $k$ marked plots are distinct because each step moves past at least one unselected plot. Reading the gaps off this selection returns the original tuple, and building the selection from the tuple returns the original $S$. So the correspondence is one-to-one in both directions.

**Counting the tuples.** We need the number of ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Write $n-k$ as a row of $n-k$ unit objects. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between adjacent objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cut points splits the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and each block has a size that is a positive integer. Different cut sets give different tuples, so the count is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. This is valid because $k\ge 1$ and $k\le n/2$ give $0 \le k-1 \le n-k-1$.

Therefore, for each of the $n$ labels $p$, there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ valid pairs, and
$$
k\,A(n,k) = |P| = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

**Dividing by $k$.** Since $k\ge 1$, we can divide both sides by $k$:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
This division is legitimate because $k$ is a fixed positive integer and we are solving an equation. It does not quotient out rotations. The plots have fixed distinct labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different sets and are both counted.

**Simplifying.** Since $n-2k\ge 0$, all factorials below are defined:
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
Also,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},
$$
where dividing by $n-k$ is valid because $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$. The two expressions are equal, so
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remark on $k=n/2$.** When $n$ is even and $k=n/2$, the gaps sum to $n-k=k$ and each must be at least $1$. So every gap equals $1$, which is allowed. This matches the count: $\binom{k-1}{k-1}=1$.

response:
**Claim.** Label the $n \ge 3$ plots $1, \dots, n$ around a circle, with plot $n$ adjacent to plot $1$. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets $S$ of plots such that no two plots in $S$ are adjacent, where adjacency includes the pair $\{n,1\}$. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only $0$-element selection is the empty set, so $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$, which agrees.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $P$ be the set of pairs $(S,s)$ where $S$ is a valid $k$-selection and $s\in S$ is a marked plot. Each selection has $k$ choices for $s$, so

$$
|P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$

For each $(S,s)\in P$, walk clockwise from $s$. Let $p_1=s,\ p_2,\dots,p_k$ be the selected plots in the order met, and set $p_{k+1}=p_1$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$, for $i=1,\dots,k$. Two facts follow:

- Each $g_i\ge 1$. If $g_i=0$, then $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ would be adjacent selected plots.
- $\sum_{i=1}^k g_i = n-k$, because the $n-k$ unselected plots are split among the $k$ gaps.

When $k=1$, the single gap contains all $n-1$ other plots, so $g_1=n-1$.

Let $T$ be the set of ordered tuples $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$. The map

$$
\Phi(S,s) = (s, g_1,\dots,g_k)
$$

sends $P$ into $\{1,\dots,n\}\times T$. It is a bijection. To invert it, start at $s$ and place the selected plots at clockwise offsets

$$
d_1=0,\qquad d_{i+1}=d_i+g_i+1 \quad (i=1,\dots,k-1).
$$

The offsets increase strictly and $d_k = n-(g_k+1)<n$, so they lie in one lap and are distinct. Consecutive selected offsets differ by $g_i+1\ge 2$, and the wraparound gap from $d_k$ back to $n$ is also $g_k+1\ge 2$. So the resulting set is a valid selection with $s$ selected, and walking from $s$ recovers exactly the tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Since the sum of $(g_i+1)$ over all $i$ is $(n-k)+k=n$, the walk closes after exactly one lap. Hence $\Phi$ is a bijection, and

$$
|P| = n\,|T|.
$$

*Counting $T$.* An element of $T$ is a composition of $n-k$ into $k$ positive parts. Write $n-k$ units in a row. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between consecutive units. Cutting the row into $k$ consecutive blocks of sizes $g_1,\dots,g_k$ means choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cut points. Each choice gives exactly one tuple, and each tuple gives exactly one choice. This is valid because $k\le n-k$, so $k-1\le n-k-1$. Therefore

$$
|T| = \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Combining the counts,

$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

Since $k\ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Final identity.* Since $k\le n/2$, we have $n-2k\ge 0$, so all factorials below are defined. Also $n-k\ge 1$, so dividing by $n-k$ is legitimate. Expanding both sides:

$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},
$$

$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$

The two expressions are equal, which gives

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remarks.**

- At $k=n/2$ for even $n$, $n-k=k$, so the sum of $k$ positive gaps equals $k$. The only tuple is $(1,\dots,1)$, and $\binom{k-1}{k-1}=1$. Every gap is a single unselected plot, which is allowed. For example, with $n=4$ and $k=2$, the selections are $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$, and the formula gives $\frac{4}{2}\binom{2}{2}=2$.
- No division by $n$ accounts for rotations. The plots carry fixed distinct labels, so each selection is counted once as a set of labeled plots, and the marked start $s$ is a label rather than a rotation class.

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the only selection is the empty one, so \(A(n,0)=1\). The formula also gives \(1\).

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as a start. Each selection has exactly \(k\) selected plots that could be marked, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) such pairs.

Alternatively, choose the start plot in \(n\) ways, then record the numbers \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\) of unselected plots between each selected plot and the next selected plot clockwise. Each \(g_i\) is positive because neighboring plots cannot both be selected. The gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots, so
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]
This description also works for \(k=1\): its single gap consists of all the other \(n-1\) plots.

The number of ordered positive-integer \(k\)-tuples with sum \(n-k\) is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\). To see this, arrange \(n-k\) objects in a row and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between consecutive objects as separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and every such tuple gives exactly one choice of separators.

Thus there are \(n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\) choices of a start and gap tuple. These choices correspond one-to-one with the marked selections: the start and successive gap lengths specify every selected plot clockwise, and a marked selection determines its start and all its gap lengths. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Since \(k\ge1\), division by \(k\) is legitimate. Rewriting the binomial coefficient using factorials gives
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The range \(k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) ensures \(n-k\ge k\), so these binomial coefficients are defined. When \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which is allowed. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so no quotient by rotations is taken.

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of ways to select \(k\) plots so that no two neighboring plots are selected, including the two plots at the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** When \(k=0\), the only selection is the empty selection, and the formula gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as the start. Each selection gives \(k\) such pairs, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) pairs.

To count the same pairs another way, choose the start plot in \(n\) ways. Starting there and moving clockwise, let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). If \(k=1\), this gap consists of all the other plots before returning to the start. Each \(g_i\) is positive because neighboring plots cannot both be selected, and the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

The number of ordered lists of \(k\) positive integers with this sum is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\): represent \(n-k\) as a row of objects and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them as separators. The resulting \(k\) groups give the gap sizes. Each start plot and gap list determines exactly one marked selection, including when the gaps are all one. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Expanding the factorials gives
\[
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The division by \(k\) is legitimate because each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible choices of the marked plot. The plots have fixed labels, so rotations are not identified. \(\square\)

response:
**Claim.** Arrange n ≥ 3 labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ ⌊n/2⌋, let A(n,k) be the number of k-element selections of plots in which no two selected plots are neighbors. Plot n and plot 1 count as neighbors across the circular boundary. Then

A(n,k) = n/(n−k) · C(n−k, k).

Here C(a,b) is the binomial coefficient "a choose b".

**Proof.**

*Case k = 0.* The only selection is the empty one, and it is valid because it contains no pair of plots at all. So A(n,0) = 1. The formula gives n/n · C(n,0) = 1, so the claim holds. From here on assume k ≥ 1. Then the quantity "k selected plots" is positive, and we will be able to divide by it.

*Stage 1: what we count.* Call a **marked selection** a pair (S, s), where S is a valid k-element selection and s is one of the k plots in S, called the *start*. We count marked selections in two ways.

*Stage 2: first count, by selections.* Each valid selection S has exactly k selected plots, so it can be marked in exactly k ways. Hence

number of marked selections = k · A(n,k).

This is the step that makes the later division legitimate. We are not identifying selections that look alike. We are counting every valid selection exactly k times, so dividing by k at the end recovers A(n,k).

*Stage 3: second count, by start and gaps.* Take a marked selection (S, s). Walk clockwise from s around the circle. Label the selected plots s = p₁, p₂, …, p_k in the order met. Let gᵢ be the number of unselected plots strictly between pᵢ and the next selected plot, where the next one after p_k is p₁ = s again. For k = 1 this means all n−1 other plots, since the walk returns to s without meeting another selected plot.

The tuple (g₁, …, g_k) has two properties.

- Each gᵢ ≥ 1, because two selected plots may not be neighbors. The gap g_k, which returns to the start, is included. This is exactly where the circular boundary condition is enforced. For k = 1 it holds because g₁ = n−1 ≥ 2.
- g₁ + ⋯ + g_k = n−k, because every plot is either one of the k selected plots or lies in exactly one gap.

So each marked selection yields a pair (s, g), where s is one of the n plot labels and g is a tuple of k positive integers summing to n−k.

This assignment can be reversed. Given any start label s and any such tuple g, place p₁ = s and then step clockwise past g₁ unselected plots to reach p₂, past g₂ more to reach p₃, and so on. The total number of plots passed over, counting each pᵢ and the gap after it, is Σ(gᵢ + 1) = (n−k) + k = n. So after k steps we arrive back exactly at s, without overlapping, and we get k distinct selected plots. Consecutive selected plots are separated by at least one unselected plot, including the last one and s, so the selection is valid. Reading off the gaps from the marked selection (S, s) recovers g, and building from (s, g) recovers (S, s). The two assignments are inverse to each other, so marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs (s, g).

*Stage 4: counting the tuples.* We need the number of tuples of k positive integers with sum n−k. Line up n−k identical objects in a row. There are n−k−1 internal spaces between adjacent objects. Choosing k−1 of these spaces for separators cuts the row into k nonempty blocks, and the block sizes form a tuple (g₁, …, g_k) of positive integers summing to n−k. Every such tuple arises from exactly one choice of separators. So the number of tuples is C(n−k−1, k−1).

For k = 1 there are no separators to choose, and C(n−2, 0) = 1 matches the single tuple (n−1).

*Stage 5: equate and divide.* The start can be any of the n labels, independently of the tuple, so the number of marked selections is also n · C(n−k−1, k−1). Equating the two counts,

k · A(n,k) = n · C(n−k−1, k−1).

Since k ≥ 1, we may divide by k:

A(n,k) = (n/k) · C(n−k−1, k−1).

*Stage 6: rewriting.* Expand the binomial. All factorials below are defined because n−2k ≥ 0:

(n/k) · (n−k−1)! / ((k−1)! (n−2k)!) = n · (n−k−1)! / (k! (n−2k)!).

Also, since n−k > 0 (as k ≤ n/2 and n ≥ 3),

n/(n−k) · C(n−k, k) = n/(n−k) · (n−k)! / (k! (n−2k)!) = n · (n−k−1)! / (k! (n−2k)!).

The two expressions are equal, so

A(n,k) = n/(n−k) · C(n−k, k). ∎

**Remarks.**

1. *Largest case.* When n is even and k = n/2, the gaps are k positive integers with sum n−k = k, so every gap equals 1 and there is exactly one tuple. The selections are then "every other plot", and there are n·1/k = 2 of them, matching the formula. This is allowed, since a gap of one unselected plot is enough to separate neighbors.
2. *No rotation quotient.* The plots have distinct fixed labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different selections and are both counted. The division by k above is not a symmetry quotient. It only corrects for each selection having been counted once per choice of start.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two neighboring plots are selected. Plots $n$ and $1$ are neighbors, like any other adjacent pair. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*The case $k = 0$.* The only selection is the empty one, so $A(n,0) = 1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1$.

*The case $k \ge 1$.* We count marked selections: pairs $(S, s)$ where $S$ is a valid selection of $k$ plots and $s$ is one of the plots in $S$. We count them in two ways.

*First count.* Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of marked plot, so the number of marked selections is
$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

*Second count.* Given $(S,s)$, list the selected plots in clockwise order starting at $s$, as $p_1 = s, p_2, \dots, p_k$, and set $p_{k+1} = p_1$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ going clockwise. When $k = 1$, $g_1 = n-1$, the number of all other plots. These gaps have two properties:

- Every plot is either selected or lies in exactly one gap, so $g_1 + \dots + g_k = n-k$.
- Every $g_i \ge 1$. For $k = 1$ this holds because $n \ge 3$. For $k \ge 2$, if $g_i = 0$ then $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ would be neighbors, which is forbidden. This includes the pair $p_k, p_1$ when they meet across the boundary between plots $n$ and $1$.

So $(S,s)$ determines a start label $s$ and an ordered tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

Conversely, take any start label $s$ and any such tuple. Place the first selected plot at $s$. Then repeat the following for $i = 1, \dots, k-1$: skip $g_i$ plots clockwise and select the next plot. The $k$ selected plots and the $g_1 + \dots + g_{k-1}$ plots skipped so far use up $k + (n-k-g_k) = n - g_k$ consecutive plots starting at $s$. The last $g_k$ plots before returning to $s$ are therefore unselected. The selected plots are distinct, and since every gap is at least $1$, no two of them are neighbors. The result is a valid marked selection, and reading off its start and gaps recovers the original data. Hence marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs (start label, gap tuple).

There are $n$ start labels. The number of tuples of $k$ positive integers with sum $n-k$ is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. To see this, write the $n-k$ unselected plots as a row of $n-k$ objects. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between consecutive objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces for separators cuts the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and the block sizes form a tuple. Every tuple arises from exactly one choice of separators. Since $k \le n/2$, we have $n-k-1 \ge k-1 \ge 0$, so this binomial coefficient is meaningful. The start label does not affect the number of tuples, so the second count gives $n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ marked selections.

*Dividing by $k$.* Equating the two counts,
$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
Each valid selection is counted exactly $k$ times among the marked selections, once for each choice of marked plot. Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Rewriting the coefficient.* Expanding the binomial coefficient,
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
On the other hand, since $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
The two expressions agree, so $A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

1. When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, the sum $n-k = k$ forces every gap to equal $1$. This is allowed, because gaps only need to be positive. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n/2}\binom{n/2}{n/2} = 2$, matching the two alternating selections.
2. We never divide by rotations of the circle. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so selections that differ by a rotation are different selections, and the $n$ choices of start label are all counted.

**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two neighboring plots are selected. Plots 1 and $n$ (or whichever two plots meet at the circular boundary) count as neighbors. Then
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*The case $k=0$.* The only selection is the empty one, and it is valid because it contains no pair of plots. So $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$.

*The case $k \ge 1$.* A selection on a circle has no natural starting point, and we need one to list the gaps between selected plots in order. So we count marked selections, meaning pairs $(S,s)$ where $S$ is a valid selection of $k$ plots and $s$ is one of the plots in $S$. We count these pairs in two ways.

*First count.* Each valid selection has exactly $k$ selected plots, so it can be marked in $k$ ways. The number of marked selections is therefore
$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

*Second count.* Take a marked selection $(S,s)$. Walk clockwise around the circle starting at $s$, and call the selected plots $s_1=s, s_2, \dots, s_k$ in the order we meet them. For $i=1,\dots,k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots between $s_i$ and the next selected plot, where the next selected plot after $s_k$ is $s$ itself. For $k=1$, $g_1$ is the number of all the other plots, namely $n-1$. This gives:

* Each $g_i \ge 1$, because two selected plots that follow each other around the circle cannot be neighbors. This includes the pair $s_k$ and $s$ across the boundary. (For $k=1$, $g_1=n-1\ge 2$.)
* $g_1+\cdots+g_k = n-k$, because every unselected plot lies in exactly one of the gaps.

So $(S,s)$ produces a start plot $s$, which can be any of the $n$ plots, together with a $k$-tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers summing to $n-k$.

Conversely, suppose we are given any plot $s$ and any such tuple. Select $s$, walk clockwise past $g_1$ unselected plots, and select the next plot. Continue in the same way through $g_2,\dots,g_{k-1}$, select the $k$-th plot, and then walk past $g_k$ unselected plots. The walk takes
$$
\sum_{i=1}^k (g_i+1) = (n-k)+k = n
$$
steps, so it arrives back at $s$ after going around the circle exactly once. This means the $k$ selected plots are distinct. Since every gap is at least 1, no two selected plots are neighbors, including $s_k$ and $s$. So we obtain a valid marked selection. The two constructions undo each other, so marked selections correspond exactly to pairs consisting of a start plot and a tuple of gaps.

*Counting the tuples.* Put the $n-k$ unselected plots in a row. A tuple of $k$ positive integers with sum $n-k$ is the same as a way of cutting this row into $k$ nonempty consecutive blocks, where the block sizes are $g_1,\dots,g_k$. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between adjacent objects in the row, and a cut uses $k-1$ of them. Choosing which spaces to cut gives
$$
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
$$
tuples. Since $k\le n/2$, we have $n-k\ge k$, so there is at least one tuple.

*Combining the two counts.* The start plot can be chosen in $n$ ways, independently of the tuple. Counting marked selections both ways gives
$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Why we may divide by $k$.* The left side counts each valid selection exactly $k$ times, once for each choice of marked plot, and $k\ge 1$. Dividing by $k$ therefore gives the number of selections themselves:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Rewriting.* Since $n-k \ge k$, we can write
$$
\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n-k}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n-k}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
Because $n-k>0$, we can solve for the last binomial coefficient and substitute:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1} = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

*Remarks.* When $n$ is even and $k=n/2$, every gap equals 1, which is allowed, and the formula gives $A(n,n/2)=2$: the two alternating selections. We never divide by $n$ or identify selections that differ by a rotation, because the plots have distinct fixed labels, so a rotated selection is a different selection. The factor $n$ in the proof counts the possible start plots. $\blacksquare$
