The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. "Heavy rain this morning" is useful. "The heap has entered a troubled period" is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.

It does not mean that the initial value was accurate. We did not place a certified reference mass on the balance during this check.

The same sealed container remained on the pan throughout. This avoids variability from replacing the container, but it also means that the check says nothing about repeatability after unloading and reloading. The maintenance record should preserve that distinction.

The room temperature recorded at the start and end was the same to the wall sensor's displayed precision. There were no readings between those times. We therefore cannot exclude a temporary temperature change during the observation period, nor can we determine whether such a change would have affected this balance. The temperature record is context for the check, not a correction applied to the mass readings.

No visible condensation appeared on the container. That observation does not measure moisture exchange, because the check included neither a humidity measurement nor an independent mass reference. We report it to describe what the operator saw, not to establish a mechanism for the stable display.

These results support a narrow entry in the maintenance log: no displayed drift beyond the stated tolerance during this placement and observation period. A calibration decision would require the separate reference-mass procedure.

# Map Archive: Changes to Retrieval During the Trial

For the next six weeks, the map archive will run a trial change to how requested material is retrieved. The reading room will keep its usual opening hours, and access to the collection is unchanged. What changes is when requests are collected from the store.

**How retrieval works during the trial**

- Requests received before noon are collected together and retrieved at 2 p.m.
- There is no second afternoon retrieval during the trial.

**You do not need to arrive before noon**

- If you have requested a map in advance, you can arrive later in the day.
- If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves.
- To request an item for the next opening day, submit the request before noon. It is the request that must arrive before noon, not you.

**Requests must include a shelfmark**

- A request that includes a shelfmark will join the 2 p.m. retrieval.
- A request without a shelfmark will be held while staff help identify the item. It will join the next retrieval after identification, which may not be on the day the request was first received.

**Fragile maps**

- Maps already identified as fragile require a support prepared by the conservation team. The conservation team will contact you to arrange an appointment.
- The 2 p.m. retrieval does not apply to these appointments.
- The catalogue will identify affected maps. If an item is found to need support during retrieval, staff will contact you.

**About the trial**

The trial is intended to reduce interruptions in the store. It does not reduce opening hours. We will count delayed requests and review reader comments before deciding whether to continue. A comment card is available at the desk throughout the trial.

## Map archive retrieval trial

For the next six weeks, the reading room will keep its usual opening times. The trial changes how material is retrieved, not who can use the archive or when they can arrive.

Requests received before noon will be collected for retrieval at 2 p.m. There will be no second retrieval in the afternoon. You do not need to arrive before noon: if you have requested a map in advance, you can arrive later. If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you may submit a request for the next opening day.

Your request must arrive before noon and include a shelfmark to be included in that day’s retrieval. Requests without a shelfmark will be held while staff help identify the item. Once identified, they will join the next retrieval; this may be on a later day.

Maps already identified as fragile need a support prepared by the conservation team. The team will contact you to arrange an appointment. These appointments are not part of the 2 p.m. retrieval. The catalogue will identify maps known to need support, but a map may also be found to need support during retrieval. In that case, staff will contact you.

The trial is intended to reduce interruptions in the store; it does not reduce opening hours. We will count delayed requests and review reader comments before deciding whether to continue. Comment cards will be available at the desk throughout the trial.

response:
# Map Archive: Trial Change to Retrieval

For the next six weeks, the map archive will trial a different arrangement for retrieving material. The reading room will keep its usual opening times. The change affects retrieval, not access. Access has sometimes been taken to mean that every item can be brought upstairs immediately, and during the trial that will not be the case.

## How to request a map

- **Requests received before noon** will be collected together and retrieved at two o'clock.
- **There will be no second afternoon retrieval** during the trial.
- **Include a shelfmark.** A request needs a shelfmark to join the retrieval.

You do not need to arrive before noon. It is the request that must arrive by then, not you. If you have requested a map in advance, you can come later in the day. If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you can submit a request for the next opening day.

## Requests without a shelfmark

Requests without a shelfmark will be held while staff help you identify the item. Once it is identified, the request will join the next retrieval. That may not be on the day the request was first received.

## Fragile maps

Maps already identified as fragile need a support prepared by the conservation team. The team will contact you with an appointment, and the two o'clock retrieval does not apply to these appointments.

The catalogue shows which maps are affected. Occasionally an item is found to need support only when staff retrieve it. In that case, staff will contact you.

## Why we are doing this

The trial is intended to reduce interruptions in the store. It is not a reduction in opening hours. Before deciding whether to continue, we will count delayed requests and review reader comments. A comment card will be available at the desk throughout the trial, and we welcome your views.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller, but it does not establish whether the room is too humid or the probe is giving an unreliable reading. The other display, often called the “backup,” measures temperature only, so a normal reading there cannot resolve a question about humidity.

On all three mornings, the amber indicator cleared within twelve minutes. Operators wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing on two mornings; on the third, nobody touched it. These observations are consistent with moisture around the housing, but they do not establish that wiping cleared the warning. The housing is not the sensing element. Wiping is recorded here as an observation, not recommended as a remedy.

For now, record when the indicator appears, when it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator remains amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may request a handheld humidity check using the unit in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not authorize a restart; that decision remains with the shift lead.

Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop. This request does not establish that the seal has failed. Continue recording mornings when no warning appears by marking the “no warning” box beside the log’s time fields. Recording both warnings and mornings without warnings is necessary to show how often the pattern occurs.

response:
Rain can alter a recording as well as animal calling, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changed the output of a fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance; calling activity itself is an ecological outcome only when it matches the study question.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, with shield status assigned to the two positions by a coin toss. The devices recorded simultaneously, and detector settings remained fixed. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, yielding 144 paired windows. Field logs classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry; weather was not experimentally assigned. A recording was classified as positive when the detector marked at least one target call.

In wet conditions, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. Of the discordant pairs, twelve were positive only on the shielded device and seven only on the exposed device. In dry conditions, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both joint positives and joint negatives, which were not separated in this summary. The agreement counts therefore cannot be interpreted as counts of windows containing calls.

The direction of discordance differed between the observed weather categories: shield-only positives exceeded exposed-only positives in wet windows, whereas exposed-only positives slightly exceeded shield-only positives in dry windows. This pattern is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Without independent call labeling, however, it cannot show whether the additional positives represented genuine calls or detection errors. Nor does it establish that rain reduced calling. Weather was observational, and repeated windows within patches mean that the 144 paired windows were not 144 independent ecological replicates.

The pilot thus identifies a measurement question that should be addressed before these recordings are used to infer ecological trends. Blinded human labeling could help distinguish genuine calls from detection errors, and sampling more patches could broaden the comparison. For the present data, the supported conclusion is descriptive: the paired devices showed different patterns of discordance in wet and dry windows, while the biological interpretation remains unresolved.

Rain may change what a recorder captures as well as how much animals call, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. Changes in calling are themselves of ecological interest when calling is the quantity the study aims to measure. Our pilot examined whether a rain shield changes the output of one fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, and used a coin toss to assign their positions within each patch. The devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. Field logs classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned. A recording was counted as positive when the detector marked at least one target call, using the same detector settings throughout.

During wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in twelve pairs, and the exposed device alone in seven. During dry windows, they agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both pairs in which both devices were positive and pairs in which neither was positive. Because this summary does not separate those outcomes, the agreement counts cannot be read as the number of windows with calls.

The excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives during wet windows is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Without independent call labels, however, we cannot determine whether the shield recovered genuine calls. The comparison also does not establish that rain reduced calling. Although there were 144 paired windows, repeated observations within the twelve patches do not constitute independent ecological replicates. The data describe disagreement between the devices, but leave its biological interpretation unresolved.

This pilot identifies a measurement question to address before using the recordings to infer ecological trends. A future study could include blinded human labeling and more patches. This matters when comparing wet and dry surveys, because a change in detections could reflect the recording, the calling, or both. Calling is the ecological quantity of interest only if the question concerns calling. This pilot asked a narrower question: does a rain shield change the output of one fixed call detector? We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. The field log classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned, so the wet/dry contrast is observational. A window was scored positive if the detector marked at least one target call, and detector settings were identical throughout.

**Results.** Table 1 gives the paired outcomes by weather category.

| Weather | Pairs | Devices agreed | Shield-only positive | Exposed-only positive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wet | 48 | 29 | 12 | 7 |
| Dry | 96 | 84 | 5 | 7 |

Disagreement was thus 19 of 48 pairs in wet windows and 12 of 96 in dry windows. In wet windows, shield-only positives exceeded exposed-only positives (12 vs. 7). In dry windows the direction was slightly reversed (5 vs. 7). "Agreed" combines pairs in which both devices were positive with pairs in which neither was, and we have not separated these here. The agreement counts therefore cannot be read as the number of windows containing calls.

**Interpretation.** The wet-window excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Several limits apply:

- No independent labeling of calls was done, so the data cannot show that the shield recovered genuine calls rather than, for example, producing different false positives.
- The data do not show that rain reduced calling. Both devices sat in the same patch at the same time, and the comparison concerns how they differ in detector output, not how much the animals called.
- The 144 windows are repeated measures within twelve patches and are not independent ecological replicates. The effective sample is closer to the number of patches, and the discordant counts are small.

response:
The persistence rule detected more induced valve faults than the comparison rule in the held-out bench evaluation, but it also produced more alarms in cycles with no induced fault. Although transient pressure spikes motivated the persistence requirement, the results do not demonstrate improved false-alarm control.

The persistence rule requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before raising an alarm. The comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording; the evaluation recordings were not used to select them. The rules therefore differ in both threshold and persistence requirement. The lower threshold changes which cycles can trigger an alarm, so the observed differences cannot be attributed to persistence alone.

The held-out set comprised 120 cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule could produce at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarmed in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles, compared with 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles for the comparison rule. Thus, the persistence rule detected more induced faults at the cost of more alarms in cycles designated no-fault. This designation means only that no fault was induced; the machine was not dismantled after every cycle to exclude all possible defects.

Eighteen fault cycles triggered both rules. Within this shared subset, the mean time from logged fault onset to the first alarm was 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Comparing delays on the same cycles avoids differences arising from the composition of the detection sets. However, it excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both. The shorter mean delay therefore applies only to the shared detections.

These findings distinguish the rule’s motivation from its observed benefit. Requiring repeated crossings was intended to address transient spikes, but the demonstrated benefit was higher detection of induced faults, accompanied by more alarms in no-fault cycles. A low threshold combined with a persistence condition does not, by construction alone, establish better false-alarm control.

The evaluation compares two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. It does not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. Neither rule has been selected as preferred: that choice depends on the relative costs of missed faults and cycle interruptions, which were not measured.

response:
The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season because it better fits the exhibit’s existing question: how does a reading change when an instrument is tilted? Visitors cannot tilt the original. The original’s availability on loan is a valuable opportunity that may not recur, but availability alone does not determine which object best serves the exhibit we have designed.

The original offers something the replica cannot: a material connection to the instrument’s working history. A maker’s correction remains visible on its scale, providing a basis for exploring repair and adaptation. A photograph would not give every visitor the same experience as standing beside that object. Our current text, however, centers on reading and error. Making the original’s history central would require a change in direction and a different use of the season’s remaining preparation time. If the committee prefers that approach, it should explicitly authorize the redesign.

Cost supports the choice of the replica but does not make the loan untenable. The quoted loan cost is 18,000 units, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case; the replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Both fit the allocated budget, and neither quote fully accounts for staff time. The reason to prefer the replica is therefore what visitors would be permitted to do, with its lower quoted cost leaving more resources available for testing the activity.

That testing remains necessary. A replica is not automatically an effective teaching object: its moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the scale. The proposed activity has not yet been tried with visitors, so we cannot claim that handling improves understanding. We can say that the replica permits the activity the exhibit calls for, and a visitor trial would help establish whether that activity works as intended.

Choosing the replica now would align the object with the existing question while preserving resources to test the activity. We should retain a clearly labeled photograph of the original and explain why the replica can be handled. This recommendation rests on the exhibit’s current direction; choosing the original would be reasonable if the committee also chooses to make its working history the central question.

# Recommendation: Handling Replica for the Navigation Exhibit

The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season. The original instrument is available on loan, and declining it may mean giving up an opportunity that does not recur. That loss is real, but availability alone does not determine which object serves the exhibit we have designed. The exhibit asks visitors to work out how a reading changes when an instrument is tilted. Visitors cannot tilt the original, so the original cannot support the question as currently framed.

**Costs.** The loan would cost 18,000 units from the exhibit budget, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case. The handling replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Both options fit the allocated budget, so this recommendation does not rest on affordability. These are quoted costs and do not include a full estimate of staff time, which would differ between the two options.

**Why the replica fits the question.** The central reason for preferring the replica is what visitors would be permitted to do. Handling the instrument lets visitors tilt it and compare readings directly, which is the action the exhibit's question depends on. A photograph of the original could show the instrument but would not let visitors test the relationship between tilt and reading.

**What the original offers.** The original has something the replica cannot provide: a material connection to the instrument's working history. A maker's correction remains visible on its scale. That detail could support an account of repair and adaptation, and standing beside the object would give visitors an experience a photograph cannot match. However, our current text is organized around reading and error rather than repair. Redesigning it around repair would be a different use of the season's remaining preparation time, and the committee should weigh that cost against the gain.

**Limits of the replica.** A replica is not automatically a good teaching object. Its moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the difference in scale. The proposed activity therefore still needs a trial with visitors. That trial has not yet taken place, so this recommendation does not claim that handling has improved understanding. The trial is a condition for judging whether the replica works, not a formality.

**Proposed course.** Choose the handling replica now. This matches the object to the existing question and keeps resources available for testing the activity with visitors. Retain a clearly labeled photograph of the original in the exhibit, and explain to visitors why the replica can be handled while the original cannot.

**Alternative.** If the committee instead wants the original's history to be the central question, it should explicitly authorize that change in the exhibit's direction. That choice would also require the redesign of the text around repair and would change how the season's preparation time is spent.

response:
We recommend a limited trial of revised discovery labels for twenty digitized collections. Some existing labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories they were. The proposal would change the short descriptions that help readers decide which collection to open. The scanned inventories would remain available exactly as they are.

The distinction matters: revising a discovery label does not alter the historical document. Yet a label is also part of how the archive represents a collection, so its wording cannot be treated as mere packaging. The question is how to describe the material now while preserving access through the language of the original inventories.

The existing labels offer a real retrieval benefit. Readers following quotations from an inventory can recognize the same words in the catalogue. Readers who have not seen the inventory, however, may take those words as the archive’s present description. Repeating an old heading can therefore serve one route into the material while misleading readers on another. Both needs deserve consideration.

We propose a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original heading, and retention of that heading as a searchable alternative. Historical quotations would remain a route into the collection, without the quoted wording having to stand alone as its present description. Search results would display the current label; the note would be visible when a reader opened the record. The original wording would also remain unchanged in the scanned inventory.

One objection is that a replacement label interprets the collection. It does. But selecting an inventory heading as the main discovery label is also an interpretive choice, even when it appears simply to copy the source. Recognizing this does not make every replacement equally sound. A new label should describe the contents at the level the collection supports, and its accompanying note should make the relationship to the old wording visible. Labels have been drafted for the twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not yet reviewed them.

A second objection concerns readability: adding historical context can make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record preserves concise search results, but it also means that readers may not immediately see the historical wording they recognize. The proposal therefore makes a tradeoff between immediate recognition and a current description with context available in the record. It does not fully satisfy both needs at every point of discovery.

That unresolved tradeoff supports a trial rather than wider adoption. The trial should be followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that the changes will improve retrieval; the purpose is to test whether they can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before that check would go beyond what the present case supports.

response:
Our proposal concerns the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. Several of these labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without saying whose categories those headings were. The scanned inventories would remain available exactly as they are. What changes is the text that helps a reader decide which collection to open. That text is not mere packaging. It is part of how the archive represents each collection, so it has to be justified on those terms.

The case for the existing labels should be stated fully before we depart from them. Matching the old headings has a real retrieval benefit. A reader following a quotation from an inventory can recognize the same words in the catalogue and find the collection the quotation came from. The headings also preserve a visible link to the historical vocabulary.

The difficulty is that one label does two jobs. For a reader who has the inventory in hand, it points back to a source. For a reader who has not seen the inventory, it reads as the archive's present description of what the collection contains and how it is classified. Repeating the heading can therefore be faithful to one route through the material while misleading on another. Neither route is imaginary, and the proposal has to serve both.

This is why we separate two things that are easily run together. Changing a discovery label changes how a collection is found and described at the point of selection. Changing a historical record would alter the document itself: what it says and how it stands as evidence. The proposal changes only the first. The inventories stay as they are, and the old heading stays in the catalogue as a searchable term. What it no longer does is serve as the main description.

Concretely, we propose three elements: a current descriptive label; a note identifying the original heading and the categories it reflects; and the original heading retained as a searchable alternative. Quoted words still lead into the collection, but they do not have to stand alone as its present description. Search results would show the current label. The note would appear when a reader opens the record, so the historical wording is not hidden, only placed beside an account of where it came from.

The first objection is that any replacement label interprets the collection. We accept this. Keeping the old heading as the main label is also an interpretation, one that merely looks like copying. But accepting that every label is interpretive does not make every replacement equally sound. A new label should describe the contents at the level the collection supports, and the note should make the relationship to the old wording explicit. The drafted labels have not yet been reviewed by readers or subject specialists, so they should be treated as provisional.

The second objection is that notes make a short catalogue harder to scan. This is a real cost. Because the note sits inside the record, a reader scanning search results may not see the historical wording immediately. We do not claim this dissolves the competing needs. It is a tradeoff, and the trial is designed to show how it plays out rather than to assume the answer.

We therefore recommend a limited trial on these twenty collections, with checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that the trial will improve retrieval, and we do not present it as having done so. Its purpose is narrower: to test whether current labels with visible notes give readers context while keeping a route from historical quotations into the collections. Expanding the policy before that check would outrun the present case for it.

The proposal changes the text that helps readers decide which collection to open; it does not change the scanned inventories, which would remain available exactly as they are. Still, a discovery label is part of how the archive represents a collection, not merely packaging, so revising it deserves care.

The existing labels have a genuine advantage: they match the old headings, helping readers who arrive through a quotation from an inventory recognize the same words in the catalogue. But a reader who has not seen that inventory may take the label as the archive’s present description. Repeating the heading can therefore support one route into the material while misleading readers on another. Both uses matter.

Our proposal is to provide a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original heading, and the original heading as a searchable alternative. This keeps the quoted words as a route into the collection without asking them to serve alone as its present description. The historical wording would remain in the scanned document and in the searchable alternative; search results would show the current label, with the note visible when a reader opens the record.

One objection is that any replacement label interprets the collection. We agree. Choosing an inventory heading as the main label also interprets it, even when that choice looks like copying. But recognizing that both choices involve interpretation does not make them equally good. A replacement should describe the contents only at the level the collection supports, and the note should make its relationship to the old wording visible. We have drafted labels for the twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not yet reviewed them.

A second objection is that notes make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record addresses that concern, but means readers scanning search results may not immediately see the historical wording. This is a real tradeoff: the proposal preserves a route from historical quotations, but does not make every piece of context visible at every stage.

We therefore recommend trying the approach with the twenty collections and checking both successful and failed searches. We do not yet have evidence that the trial will improve retrieval. Its purpose is to test whether this way of providing context can preserve a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before those checks would go beyond the case we can currently make.

response:
Let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\) be the initial sensor value, and let \(\delta_k\in\mathbb R\) be the correction at step \(k\). Suppose that, for some \(A\ge 0\),
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]
Define the cumulative corrected values by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k
\qquad(n\ge 0),
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). Then \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\), and the remaining correction after step \(m\) satisfies
\[
\boxed{|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}}
\qquad(m\ge 0).
\]

**Proof.** For integers \(n>m\ge 0\), the difference \(c_n-c_m\) consists precisely of the corrections from step \(m\) through step \(n-1\). The triangle inequality and the assumed bound therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}
\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)
\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The telescoping identity shows that the total change between any two sufficiently late steps is small, independently of how many corrections lie between them.

Indeed, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(M\ge 0\) such that \(A/(M+1)<\varepsilon\). If \(n>m\ge M\), the estimate above yields \(|c_n-c_m|<\varepsilon\). The same conclusion holds when \(m>n\) by interchanging the indices, and when \(m=n\) the difference is zero. Thus \((c_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence. Completeness of \(\mathbb R\) supplies a finite limit \(c\).

To obtain the quantitative bound, fix \(m\) and let \(n\to\infty\) in
\[
|c_n-c_m|
\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
\]
Continuity of absolute value gives
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\]
When \(A=0\), every correction vanishes, so \(c=c_0\). Throughout the argument, corrections may have either sign: the bound controls their absolute tails and requires no monotonicity of the cumulative values. \(\square\)

Let \(A\ge 0\), let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\), and suppose the real corrections \(\delta_k\) satisfy
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad (k\ge 0).
\]
Define the cumulative corrected value by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k
\qquad (n\ge 0),
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). We show that \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\) and that
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\qquad (m\ge 0).
\]

For integers \(n>m\ge 0\), the difference \(c_n-c_m\) consists of the corrections with indices \(m,\ldots,n-1\). By the triangle inequality and the assumed bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}
  \left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate equality follows because all intermediate terms cancel.

This estimate shows that cumulative values become arbitrarily close once both indices are sufficiently large. Indeed, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(M\ge 0\) such that
\[
\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
For \(n>m\ge M\), we then have
\[
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\le \frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The same conclusion holds when \(m>n\) by interchanging the indices, and when \(m=n\) the difference is zero. Thus \((c_n)\) is Cauchy. Completeness of \(\mathbb R\) gives a finite limit \(c\).

To obtain the error bound, fix \(m\ge 0\) and let \(n\to\infty\) in the sharper estimate above. Continuity of absolute value gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c-c_m|
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n-c_m|\\
&\le \lim_{n\to\infty}
A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&=\frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corrections may have either sign, and neither they nor the cumulative values need be monotone: the proof bounds the sum of the absolute corrections. If \(A=0\), every correction is zero, so \(c_n=c=c_0\) for all \(n\).

**Proposition.** Let $A \ge 0$ and $c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $(\delta_k)_{k\ge 0}$ be real numbers satisfying

$$
|\delta_k| \le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)} \qquad (k \ge 0).
$$

Define $c_n = c_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \delta_k$ for $n \ge 1$, with $c_0$ as the value at $n = 0$ (the empty sum). Then $(c_n)$ converges to a real number $c$, and

$$
|c - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1} \qquad \text{for every integer } m \ge 0.
$$

The corrections may be positive, negative, or mixed in sign.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: Bounding a tail.* Fix integers $n > m \ge 0$. Subtracting the defining sums gives

$$
c_n - c_m = \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \delta_k,
$$

since the terms $k = 0, \dots, m-1$ cancel. The triangle inequality for finite sums and the hypothesis on each $\delta_k$ give

$$
|c_n - c_m| \le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} |\delta_k| \le A \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$

*Step 2: Telescoping.* For each $k$, the partial-fraction identity

$$
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} = \frac{1}{k+1} - \frac{1}{k+2}
$$

holds, since the right side equals $\dfrac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+1)(k+2)}$. Substituting and noting that consecutive terms cancel,

$$
\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \left( \frac{1}{k+1} - \frac{1}{k+2} \right) = \frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{n+1}.
$$

Therefore

$$
|c_n - c_m| \le A\left( \frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right) \le \frac{A}{m+1}, \tag{1}
$$

where the last step uses $A \ge 0$ and $1/(n+1) \ge 0$. Inequality (1) is the key estimate. It bounds the tail of the sequence after index $m$ by a quantity depending only on $m$ and $A$, not on $n$.

*Step 3: The sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $A$ is a fixed real number and $1/(M+1) \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$, there is an integer $M \ge 0$ with

$$
\frac{A}{M+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

(If $A = 0$, any $M$ works.) Let $m, n \ge M$. If $n > m$, then by (1),

$$
|c_n - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1} \le \frac{A}{M+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

If $m > n$, the same argument with the roles reversed applies. If $m = n$, then $|c_n - c_m| = 0 < \varepsilon$. Hence $|c_n - c_m| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \ge M$, so $(c_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

*Step 4: Existence of the limit.* Since $\mathbb{R}$ is complete, every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. So there is a real number $c$ with $c_n \to c$.

*Step 5: The error bound.* Fix $m \ge 0$. By (1), for every $n > m$,

$$
|c_n - c_m| \le A\left( \frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right).
$$

As $n \to \infty$, the left side tends to $|c - c_m|$ by continuity of the absolute value, since $c_n \to c$ implies $|c_n - c_m| \to |c - c_m|$. The right side tends to $A/(m+1)$. Passing to the limit in the inequality preserves it, so

$$
|c - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1}.
$$

*Remarks.*

1. **Sign of the corrections.** The argument never uses the sign of any $\delta_k$. Only $|\delta_k|$ enters, through the triangle inequality in Step 1. The bound therefore holds for arbitrary sign patterns.

2. **No monotonicity.** Neither the corrections nor the partial sums $c_n$ are assumed monotone. The estimate controls the absolute tails $|c_n - c_m|$ directly, and that suffices for Cauchy-ness.

3. **The degenerate case $A = 0$.** Then every $\delta_k$ vanishes, so $c_n = c_0$ for all $n$. The sequence is constant, its limit is $c = c_0$, and the bound reads $|c - c_m| = 0 \le 0$. This is consistent with the general argument. Step 3 holds with any $M$, and Step 5 gives $|c - c_m| \le 0$ directly.

4. **Interpretation.** The proof shows that the total accumulated correction is controlled by a tail of a convergent telescoping series. After $m$ corrections have been applied, the remaining uncertainty about the limit is at most $A/(m+1)$. This is the quantitative content an appendix on cumulative sensor corrections needs: the error decays like $1/m$ and is explicit in terms of the correction bound $A$.

$\blacksquare$

$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}\qquad(k\ge 0).
$$

$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{for every integer } m\ge 0.
$$
The corrections may have either sign. The argument uses only their absolute values.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: Partial fractions.* For each $k\ge 0$,
$$
\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}=\frac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$

*Step 2: A bound on tails.* Let $n>m\ge 0$. In $c_n-c_m$, the constant $c_0$ cancels, and so do the terms $\delta_k$ with $k<m$. Therefore
$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k.
$$
By the triangle inequality and the hypothesis on $\delta_k$,
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$
By Step 1, the sum telescopes. Each term $-\frac{1}{k+2}$ cancels the term $\frac{1}{(k+1)+1}$ from the next index, so only the first and last terms survive:
$$
A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
$$
The last term is $-\frac{1}{(n-1)+2}=-\frac{1}{n+1}$. Since $A\ge 0$ and $\frac{1}{n+1}>0$, we get
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad(n>m\ge 0). \tag{1}
$$

*Step 3: The sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, there is an integer $M\ge 0$ with $A/(M+1)<\varepsilon$. (If $A=0$, any $M$ works.) Take integers $p,q\ge M$, and set $m=\min(p,q)$ and $n=\max(p,q)$.

- If $p=q$, then $|c_p-c_q|=0<\varepsilon$.
- If $p\ne q$, then $n>m\ge M$, and by (1),
$$
|c_p-c_q|=|c_n-c_m|\le\frac{A}{m+1}\le\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

So $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Since $\mathbb R$ is complete, there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$.

*Step 4: The error bound.* Fix $m\ge 0$. By (1), $|c_n-c_m|\le A/(m+1)$ for every $n>m$. The left side is a continuous function of $c_n$, and $c_n\to c$, so $|c_n-c_m|\to|c-c_m|$ as $n\to\infty$. Non-strict inequalities survive limits, so
$$
|c-c_m|\le\frac{A}{m+1}.
$$

*Remark on $A=0$.* In this case the hypothesis forces $\delta_k=0$ for all $k$. Then $c_n=c_0$ for every $n$, so $c=c_0$, and the bound reads $|c_0-c_m|=0\le 0$. This agrees with the general argument.

**Lemma.** Let $A\ge 0$, let $c_0\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\delta_k\in\mathbb{R}$ for each integer $k\ge 0$ satisfy

$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}\qquad (k\ge 0).
$$

Define $c_0$ as given and, for $n\ge 1$,

$$
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k .
$$

For $n=0$ the empty sum is zero, so this formula also gives $c_0$. Then the sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge 0}$ converges to a real number $c$, and for every integer $m\ge 0$,

$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
$$

The corrections $\delta_k$ may be positive or negative. The argument below uses no monotonicity of the corrections or of the partial sums. It controls only the absolute size of each correction, and that is enough to control the absolute tails of the sequence.

**Step 1: Bound the difference of two partial sums.**

Let $n>m\ge 0$. The terms with $k<m$ appear in both $c_n$ and $c_m$, so they cancel:

$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k .
$$

This also holds when $m=0$, since then $c_0$ is the empty sum. By the triangle inequality and the hypothesis on $\delta_k$,

$$
|c_n-c_m|
\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|
\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} .
$$

We evaluate the last sum with a partial fraction decomposition. Since

$$
\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}=\frac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)},
$$

we have

$$
\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}
=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right).
$$

In this sum, each term $-\frac{1}{k+2}$ cancels the term $+\frac{1}{(k+1)+1}$ from the next index. Only the first term $\frac{1}{m+1}$ and the last term $-\frac{1}{n+1}$ survive, so

$$
\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)=\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}.
$$

Combining these displays gives

$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\tag{1}
$$

The last inequality holds because $A\ge 0$ and $\frac{1}{n+1}\ge 0$.

If $n=m$, then $|c_n-c_m|=0$, so the same bound holds trivially. If $m>n$, exchange the roles of $n$ and $m$. Therefore, for any integers $n,m\ge M\ge 0$,

$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{M+1}.
\tag{2}
$$

To see this, assume without loss of generality that $n\ge m\ge M$. Then (1) gives $|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}$, and $\frac{A}{m+1}\le \frac{A}{M+1}$ because $m\ge M$.

**Step 2: The sequence is Cauchy.**

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, we can choose an integer $M\ge 0$ with

$$
\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon .
$$

By (2), every pair of indices $n,m\ge M$ satisfies $|c_n-c_m|<\varepsilon$. This is the Cauchy condition. Since the real numbers are complete, every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges, so there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$.

**Step 3: The error bound.**

Fix $m\ge 0$. For every $n>m$, inequality (1) gives

$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
$$

Now let $n\to\infty$. Since $c_n\to c$, the reverse triangle inequality gives

$$
\bigl|\,|c_n-c_m|-|c-c_m|\,\bigr|\le |c_n-c|\to 0,
$$

so $|c_n-c_m|\to |c-c_m|$. The right-hand side tends to $A/(m+1)$, because $1/(n+1)\to 0$. Limits preserve non-strict inequalities, so

$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
$$

This holds for every integer $m\ge 0$. In particular, after $m$ corrections, the partial sum $c_m$ lies within $A/(m+1)$ of the limit $c$.

**Remark on the case $A=0$.** If $A=0$, the hypothesis forces $\delta_k=0$ for every $k$. Then $c_n=c_0$ for all $n$, so $c=c_0$. This agrees with the bound, which gives $|c-c_m|\le 0$ for every $m$.

\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad(m\ge 0).

\[
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}

\[
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)
\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
|c-c_m|
\le \lim_{n\to\infty} A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)
=\frac{A}{m+1}.
\]

## Appendix: Convergence of cumulative corrections

**Setting.** Let $A \ge 0$ and $c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. For each integer $k \ge 0$ let $\delta_k \in \mathbb{R}$ be a correction satisfying

$$|\delta_k| \le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}. \tag{1}$$

The corrections may have either sign. Define the cumulative value after $n$ corrections by

$$c_n = c_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \delta_k \qquad (n \ge 0),$$

where the empty sum at $n=0$ gives $c_0$.

**Claim.** The sequence $(c_n)$ has a finite real limit $c$, and for every integer $m \ge 0$,

$$|c - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1}. \tag{2}$$

The idea is that the bound (1) can be summed exactly, because $\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}$ telescopes. This gives an explicit bound on how far the sequence can move after step $m$. That bound is used twice: first to show that $(c_n)$ is Cauchy, so a limit exists, and then, in the limit, to obtain (2).

### Step 1: A bound on the tail increments

Let $n > m \ge 0$. Subtracting the two defining sums leaves only the corrections with indices $m, \dots, n-1$:

$$c_n - c_m = \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \delta_k.$$

Apply the triangle inequality and then (1). Use the partial-fraction identity $\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} = \frac{1}{k+1} - \frac{1}{k+2}$, which makes the sum telescope:

$$
\begin{aligned}
|c_n - c_m|
&\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} |\delta_k|
\;\le\; A \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} \\
&= A \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} \left( \frac{1}{k+1} - \frac{1}{k+2} \right)
\;=\; A \left( \frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

Since $\frac{1}{n+1} > 0$ and $A \ge 0$, this yields the cruder bound

$$|c_n - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1} \qquad (n > m \ge 0). \tag{4}$$

No sign or monotonicity assumption on the $\delta_k$ was used. Only the absolute sizes of the corrections enter, through (1).

### Step 2: The sequence is Cauchy, so a limit exists

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\frac{A}{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$, we can choose an integer $M \ge 0$ with $\frac{A}{M+1} < \varepsilon$. (If $A = 0$, any $M$ works.)

Now let $n, m \ge M$. There are three cases:

- If $n > m$, then (4) gives $|c_n - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1} \le \frac{A}{M+1} < \varepsilon$.
- If $m > n$, the same argument with the roles of $m$ and $n$ exchanged applies, since $|c_n - c_m| = |c_m - c_n|$.
- If $n = m$, then $|c_n - c_m| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

Hence $(c_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers. By the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, it converges to some finite real number $c$.

### Step 3: The error bound for the limit

Fix $m \ge 0$. The sharper estimate (3) holds for every $n > m$:

$$|c_n - c_m| \le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{n+1}\right).$$

Let $n \to \infty$. Since $c_n \to c$ and the absolute value is continuous, the left side tends to $|c - c_m|$. On the right, $\frac{1}{n+1} \to 0$, so the right side tends to $\frac{A}{m+1}$. Limits preserve non-strict inequalities, so

$$|c - c_m| \le \frac{A}{m+1},$$

which is (2). $\blacksquare$

### Remarks

1. **The degenerate case.** If $A = 0$, then (1) forces every $\delta_k = 0$, so $c_n = c_0$ for all $n$. Then $c = c_0$, which agrees with (2).
2. **What is and is not assumed.** Neither the corrections $\delta_k$ nor the partial sums $c_n$ are assumed monotone. The argument controls the absolute size of the tails $\sum_{k \ge m} \delta_k$, which is what the bound (2) records. In particular, after $m$ corrections the cumulative value is within $\frac{A}{m+1}$ of its final value, whatever the signs of the later corrections.

$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)} .
$$

$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{for every integer } m\ge 0 .
$$
The corrections $\delta_k$ may have either sign.

*Step 1: a bound on the difference of two partial sums.* Let $n>m\ge 0$. Subtracting the two definitions leaves only the terms with indices $m,\dots,n-1$, so
$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k .
$$
Taking absolute values and applying the triangle inequality and the hypothesis on $\delta_k$ gives
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} .
$$
The summand telescopes because
$$
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

*Step 2: the sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, we can choose an integer $M\ge 0$ with $A/(M+1)<\varepsilon$. Take $n>m\ge M$. By (1),
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\le \frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon .
$$
If instead $m>n\ge M$, exchange the roles of $m$ and $n$ and use $|c_n-c_m|=|c_m-c_n|$ to get the same bound. If $m=n$ the difference is $0<\varepsilon$. Hence $|c_n-c_m|<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge M$, so $(c_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Since $\mathbb R$ is complete, there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$.

*Step 3: the error bound.* Fix $m\ge 0$. The first two lines of (1) hold for every $n>m$:
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
$$
Let $n\to\infty$. Since $c_n\to c$ and the absolute value is continuous, the left side tends to $|c-c_m|$. The right side tends to $A/(m+1)$. A non-strict inequality between convergent sequences is preserved in the limit, so
$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
$$
Since $m$ was arbitrary, this holds for every $m\ge 0$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac1{m+1}-\frac1{n+1}\right).
$$
Let $n\to\infty$. The left side tends to $|c-c_m|$, because $c_n\to c$ and the absolute value is continuous. The right side tends to $A/(m+1)$. Therefore
$$

\[

\]

\[
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
\]

\[

       \#\{\pi:S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.

# Counting Clear Tour Schedules

## Setup

There are $n$ labeled exhibit stations and $n$ labeled tour groups, both indexed by $1, \dots, n$. Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. A schedule is therefore a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, where group $i$ visits station $\pi(i)$.

A schedule is **clear** if $\pi(i) \neq i$ for every $i$. The shared labels mark pairings to avoid, such as group $i$ being assigned to station $i$. They do not describe physical positions. Nothing in the count depends on the stations being arranged in a line or a circle.

Let $D_n$ be the number of clear schedules. We prove

$$
D_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} (n-k)! = n! \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}
$$

for every integer $n \ge 0$, using $0! = 1$.

## Step 1: Detecting clear schedules with a signed sum

For a schedule $\pi$, let $F(\pi) = \{ i : \pi(i) = i \}$ be the set of groups assigned to their own labeled station. Then $\pi$ is clear exactly when $F(\pi)$ is empty.

For any finite set $F$, the signed sum over its subsets satisfies

$$
\sum_{S \subseteq F} (-1)^{|S|} = (1-1)^{|F|}.
$$

This equals $1$ when $F = \varnothing$, since the only subset is $\varnothing$ itself and its term is $1$. It equals $0$ when $F \neq \varnothing$, because the subsets pair off with opposite signs. So

$$
\sum_{S \subseteq F(\pi)} (-1)^{|S|} = \begin{cases} 1 & \pi \text{ is clear}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}
$$

## Step 2: Summing over all schedules

Add this identity over all $n!$ schedules $\pi$:

$$
D_n = \sum_{\pi} \sum_{S \subseteq F(\pi)} (-1)^{|S|}.
$$

Both sums are finite, so we may swap them. Summing over the pairs $(\pi, S)$ with $S \subseteq F(\pi)$ gives, for each fixed $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$, the sum over the schedules that fix every member of $S$:

$$
D_n = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}} (-1)^{|S|} \, \#\{\pi : S \subseteq F(\pi)\}.
$$

The condition $S \subseteq F(\pi)$ means $\pi(i) = i$ for all $i \in S$. It places no restriction on labels outside $S$. A schedule counted here may therefore fix additional labels beyond $S$. This is intended. The alternating sum is what removes these overcounts, and the signs handle every fixed point set at once.

## Step 3: Counting the schedules that fix a given set

Fix $S$ with $|S| = k$, where $0 \le k \le n$. Requiring $\pi(i) = i$ for all $i \in S$ determines $\pi$ on $S$. What remains is a bijection from the remaining $n - k$ groups to the remaining $n - k$ stations, with no constraints. There are $(n-k)!$ such bijections. Thus

$$
\#\{\pi : S \subseteq F(\pi)\} = (n-k)!.
$$

This count depends only on $|S|$. Since there are $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$, the signed sum groups by size:

$$
D_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} (n-k)!.
$$

This is the first formula. For the second, use $\binom{n}{k}(n-k)! = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} \cdot (n-k)! = \dfrac{n!}{k!}$, which gives

$$
D_n = n! \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$

## Edge cases

- **$n = 0$.** The unique empty schedule is the empty permutation. It has no group $i$ with $\pi(i) = i$, so it is clear. The formula gives $D_0 = 0! \cdot \frac{(-1)^0}{0!} = 1$, which matches. The sum has the single term $k = 0$.
- **$n = 1$.** The only schedule sends group 1 to station 1, which is forbidden. The formula gives $D_1 = 1!\left(1 - 1\right) = 0$.
- **$n = 2$.** The schedules are the identity, which fixes both labels, and the swap, which fixes neither. Only the swap is clear. The formula gives $D_2 = 2!\left(1 - 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 1$.

## Counting clear schedules

There are $n$ labeled exhibit stations and $n$ labeled tour groups, both indexed by $1,\dots,n$. Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. A schedule is therefore a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, where group $i$ visits station $\pi(i)$. Call a schedule *clear* if $\pi(i)\neq i$ for every $i$. The shared labels mark pairings to avoid. They do not describe physical positions of the stations.

Let $D_n$ be the number of clear schedules. At $n=0$, the unique empty schedule is clear, so $D_0=1$. Throughout, $0!=1$.

We will prove

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$

### Step 1: Write a clearness indicator as a sum

For a schedule $\pi$, let

$$
F(\pi)=\{\,i : \pi(i)=i\,\}
$$

be the set of groups that visit their own labeled station. Then $\pi$ is clear exactly when $F(\pi)=\varnothing$.

Consider the sum over all subsets $S$ of $F(\pi)$. Let $m=|F(\pi)|$. Since there are $\binom{m}{k}$ subsets of size $k$, the binomial theorem gives

$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{m}{k}(-1)^k
=(1-1)^{m}.
$$

If $m=0$, the only subset is $\varnothing$, and the sum is $1$, matching $(1-1)^0=1$. If $m\ge 1$, the sum is $0$. Therefore

$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \pi \text{ is clear},\\
0, & \pi \text{ is not clear}.
\end{cases}
$$

### Step 2: Swap the order of summation

Add this identity over all schedules:

$$
D_n=\sum_{\pi}\ \sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
$$

Both sums are finite, so we may interchange them. The condition $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ means exactly that $\pi(i)=i$ for every $i\in S$. Hence

$$
D_n=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{|S|}\,N(S),
\qquad
N(S)=\#\{\pi : \pi(i)=i \text{ for all } i\in S\}.
$$

The count $N(S)$ includes schedules that fix additional labels outside $S$. This is permitted, and it is why the alternating sum is needed. Each schedule is counted once for every subset of its fixed labels, and the signed sum removes exactly those schedules that have a fixed point.

### Step 3: Count $N(S)$

Let $|S|=k$. A permutation fixes every element of $S$ if and only if it maps the complement $\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus S$ onto itself and acts as the identity on $S$. On the $n-k$ remaining labels, the permutation is then an arbitrary bijection. Hence

$$
N(S)=(n-k)!.
$$

This covers the edge cases. When $k=0$, $N(\varnothing)=n!$ counts all schedules. When $k=n$, $N(S)=0!=1$, which counts the identity schedule. When $n=0$, the only subset is $\varnothing$, and $N(\varnothing)=1=0!$.

There are $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$, so

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!.
$$

### Step 4: Simplify

Since $\binom{n}{k}=\dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$,

$$
\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!}.
$$

Substituting gives

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\frac{n!}{k!}=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$

### Checks

- $n=0$: the formula gives $0!\cdot 1=1$, matching the empty schedule.
- $n=1$: $D_1=1!-1\cdot 0!=0$. The only schedule has group 1 visit station 1, so no schedule is clear.
- $n=2$: $D_2=2!-2\cdot 1!+1\cdot 0!=2-2+1=1$. The sole clear schedule swaps the two groups.

The argument uses only the fact that each schedule is a permutation of labeled stations and groups. It does not assume that the stations lie in a line or a circle.

Suppose there are $n$ labeled exhibit stations and $n$ labeled tour groups, both indexed by $1,\dots,n$. Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. Such an assignment is a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, where group $i$ visits station $\pi(i)$. Call a schedule **clear** if no group visits the station with its own label, that is, $\pi(i)\neq i$ for every $i$. The shared labels only mark pairings to avoid. They do not describe where anything sits physically.

Let $D_n$ be the number of clear schedules. We will show that for every integer $n\ge 0$,

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$

We use $0!=1$. At $n=0$, the unique empty schedule is counted, so $D_0=1$.

**Step 1: an indicator for one schedule.** For a fixed schedule $\pi$, let

$$
F(\pi)=\{\,i : \pi(i)=i\,\}
$$

be the set of groups that visit a station with their own label. Consider the alternating sum over all subsets $S\subseteq F(\pi)$:

$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}=(1-1)^{|F(\pi)|}.
$$

The equality holds because there are $\binom{|F(\pi)|}{j}$ subsets of size $j$, and the binomial theorem gives the sum. If $F(\pi)$ is empty, the only subset is the empty set, its term is $1$, and the sum is $1$. If $F(\pi)$ is nonempty, the sum is $(1-1)^{|F(\pi)|}=0$. So the sum equals $1$ when $\pi$ is clear and $0$ otherwise. Therefore

$$
\mathbf 1[\pi\text{ is clear}]=\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
$$

**Step 2: sum over all schedules.** Add this identity over all permutations $\pi$ and interchange the two finite sums:

$$
D_n=\sum_{\pi}\ \sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{|S|}\,\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.
$$

The outer sum runs over every subset $S$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The condition $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ means $\pi(i)=i$ for every $i\in S$.

**Step 3: count the inner term.** Fix a set $S$ with $|S|=k$. A permutation satisfies $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ exactly when it fixes every element of $S$. Such a permutation maps the remaining $n-k$ labels to themselves, and every permutation of those remaining labels, extended by fixing each element of $S$, is one of these permutations. So

$$
\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}=(n-k)!.
$$

This count depends only on $k$, not on which $k$-element set $S$ is chosen. There are $\binom{n}{k}$ such sets. Substituting into Step 2 gives

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!.
$$

**Step 4: the second form.** Since

$$
\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\,(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!},
$$

we have

$$
D_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$

**Edge cases and remarks.**

- A schedule counted in $\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}$ may fix labels outside $S$. This is allowed, and the count includes such schedules. It is the reason the alternating sum is needed. The terms for smaller and larger sets $S$ overcount schedules with extra fixed points, and the signs remove that overcounting.
- At $n=0$, there is one permutation, the empty one, and $F$ is empty. The formula gives $D_0=1$.
- At $n=1$, the only permutation fixes label $1$, so no schedule is clear. The formula gives $1-1=0=D_1$.
- At $n=2$, the identity fixes both labels and is not clear. The swap is the only clear schedule. The formula gives $2-2+1=1=D_2$.
- The argument uses only the labels and the permutation structure. It does not assume the stations are arranged in a line or a circle.

response:
# Counting Clear Schedules: A Readable Proof

## Setting

There are n tour groups and n exhibit stations, each labeled 1, …, n. Every group visits exactly one station, and every station receives exactly one group. A **schedule** is therefore a permutation π of {1, …, n}, where group i visits station π(i).

A schedule is **clear** if π(i) ≠ i for every i. The matching labels mark pairings to avoid (for example, group i has already seen station i). They say nothing about where stations sit in the museum.

Let D_n be the number of clear schedules.

## Claim

For every integer n ≥ 0,

D_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k · C(n,k) · (n−k)! = n! · Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k / k!,

with the convention 0! = 1. For n = 0 there is exactly one schedule, the empty one, and it counts as clear.

## Proof

**Step 1: Mark the forbidden pairings in each schedule.**
For a schedule π, let F(π) = {i : π(i) = i} be the set of groups that land on their own labeled station. A schedule is clear exactly when F(π) is empty.

**Step 2: Turn "F(π) is empty" into a number.**
Fix π and sum (−1)^{|S|} over all subsets S of F(π). Writing m = |F(π)|, there are C(m,j) subsets of size j, so

Σ_{S⊆F(π)} (−1)^{|S|} = Σ_{j=0}^{m} C(m,j)(−1)^j = (1−1)^m.

- If m ≥ 1, this equals 0.
- If m = 0, the only subset is the empty set, which contributes a single term (−1)^0 = 1. The sum is 1.

So this sum is 1 for a clear schedule and 0 for every other schedule. It acts as an indicator of clearness.

**Step 3: Add over all schedules.**
Summing the indicator over all schedules counts the clear ones:

D_n = Σ_π Σ_{S⊆F(π)} (−1)^{|S|}.

Both sums are finite (n! schedules, at most 2^n subsets each), so we may swap them. Instead of asking which subsets lie inside each F(π), we ask which schedules fix each subset S:

D_n = Σ_{S⊆{1,…,n}} (−1)^{|S|} · #{π : S ⊆ F(π)}.

**Step 4: Count the schedules that fix a given S.**
Suppose |S| = k. The condition S ⊆ F(π) says that every group in S visits its own station. That settles k groups and uses up k stations. The remaining n−k groups must be matched one-to-one with the remaining n−k stations, and any such matching works. There are (n−k)! of them.

This count includes matchings in which some of the remaining groups also land on their own stations. Such schedules fix more labels than S, which is allowed here. That is why the alternating sum is needed: a schedule with m fixed labels is counted once for each of the 2^m subsets of F(π), and Step 2 shows the signs cancel for m ≥ 1.

**Step 5: Group the subsets by size.**
There are C(n,k) subsets S of size k, and each contributes (−1)^k (n−k)!. Therefore

D_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k · C(n,k) · (n−k)!.

This is the first formula.

**Step 6: Simplify.**
Since C(n,k)(n−k)! = n!/(k!(n−k)!) · (n−k)! = n!/k!, we get

D_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k · n!/k! = n! · Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)^k / k!.

This is the second formula. ∎

## Edge Cases and Checks

- **n = 0.** There are no groups or stations and exactly one (empty) schedule. It has no fixed labels, so it is clear. The formula gives D_0 = (−1)^0 · C(0,0) · 0! = 1.
- **n = 1.** The only schedule sends group 1 to station 1, which is forbidden. The formula gives 1! − 0! = 0, so D_1 = 0.
- **n = 2.** The formula gives 2! − 2·1! + 0! = 1. The one clear schedule is the swap, with group 1 at station 2 and group 2 at station 1.
- **n = 3.** The formula gives 6 − 3·2 + 3·1 − 1 = 2. These are the two cyclic shifts.
- **Extreme values of k.** At k = 0 the only subset is the empty set, which fixes nothing, so all n! schedules are counted. At k = n, S is everything and only the identity schedule fixes it, matching (n−n)! = 0! = 1.

## Remark on Geometry

# Counting clear schedules

## Setting

There are $n$ tour groups and $n$ exhibit stations, each labeled $1,\dots,n$. Every group visits exactly one station and every station receives exactly one group, so a schedule is a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, where group $i$ visits station $\pi(i)$. A schedule is **clear** if $\pi(i)\neq i$ for every $i$. The shared labels only say which group–station pairings are to be avoided. They do not describe where the stations are in the museum.

**Claim.** For every integer $n\ge 0$, the number $D_n$ of clear schedules is

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!
= n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!},
$$

with $0!=1$. For $n=0$ the empty schedule counts as the one clear schedule.

## Proof

**Step 1: an identity that detects clear schedules.** For a schedule $\pi$, let

$$
F(\pi)=\{\,i : \pi(i)=i\,\}
$$

be the set of groups that land on the station with their own label, and let $m=|F(\pi)|$. There are $\binom{m}{j}$ subsets $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ with $|S|=j$, so the binomial theorem gives

$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^j\binom{m}{j}
=(1-1)^m .
$$

If $m\ge 1$ this equals $0$. If $F(\pi)=\varnothing$, the only subset is $S=\varnothing$ and the sum has the single term $(-1)^0=1$. Hence

$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \pi \text{ is clear},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

**Step 2: sum over all schedules.** Adding this identity over all $n!$ schedules counts each clear schedule once and every other schedule zero times:

$$
D_n=\sum_{\pi}\ \sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
$$

Both sums are finite and run over the pairs $(\pi,S)$ with $S\subseteq F(\pi)$. Condition on $S$ instead of $\pi$. The condition $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ says that $\pi$ fixes every member of $S$, so

$$
D_n=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{|S|}\,\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.
$$

**Step 3: count the schedules for a fixed $S$.** Let $|S|=k$. A schedule with $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ must send each $i\in S$ to station $i$. That uses up the $k$ stations in $S$, so the remaining $n-k$ groups must be assigned bijectively to the remaining $n-k$ stations. Every such bijection gives a valid $\pi$, so

$$
\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}=(n-k)!.
$$

This count depends only on $k$. The extreme cases are consistent. For $k=0$ it gives $n!$, all schedules. For $k=n$ it gives $0!=1$, the identity schedule.

There are $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets $S$ of size $k$, so grouping the sum in Step 2 by $k$ gives

$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!,
$$

which is the first formula.

**Step 4: the second form.** For $0\le k\le n$,

$$
\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\,(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!},
$$

and substituting this into the first formula gives

$$
D_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
\qquad\blacksquare
$$

## Remarks

**Why an alternating sum is needed.** A schedule counted in $\#\{\pi : S\subseteq F(\pi)\}$ is allowed to fix additional labels outside $S$. The count $(n-k)!$ includes those schedules. The alternating signs in Step 1 are what cancel the overcounting, so that a schedule with $m\ge1$ fixed labels contributes a total of $0$.

**Edge cases.**

- $n=0$: the only term is $k=0$, equal to $\binom{0}{0}\,0!=1$, so $D_0=1$. There are no groups, so the empty schedule has no fixed label and is clear.
- $n=1$: $D_1=1!-0!=0$. The only schedule sends group $1$ to station $1$, so none is clear.
- $n=2$: $D_2=2!-2\cdot1!+0!=1$. The schedule that swaps the two groups is the only clear one.

**Geometry.** Nothing in the argument uses the physical arrangement of the stations, whether in a line, a circle, or otherwise. Only the pairing of group labels with station labels enters the count.

## Counting clear schedules

**Setup.** There are $n$ stations and $n$ tour groups, both labeled $1,\dots,n$. Each group visits exactly one station and each station receives exactly one group, so a schedule is a permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, where group $i$ visits station $\pi(i)$. Call a schedule *clear* if $\pi(i)\neq i$ for every $i$. The shared labels only name the pairings to avoid, so the count does not depend on how the stations are physically arranged. Let $D_n$ be the number of clear schedules.

**Claim.** For every integer $n\ge 0$,
$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk (n-k)!
= n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
$$
Here $0!=1$, and for $n=0$ there is exactly one schedule, the empty one, which is clear.

**Step 1: an indicator of being clear.** For a schedule $\pi$, let
$$
F(\pi)=\{i:\pi(i)=i\}
$$
be the set of groups sent to their own-numbered station, and let $m=|F(\pi)|$. A set with $m$ elements has $\binom mj$ subsets of size $j$, so by the binomial theorem
$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^j\binom mj
=(1-1)^m .
$$
If $m=0$, the only subset is the empty set, which contributes the single term $(-1)^0=1$, so the sum is $1$. If $m\ge 1$, the right side is $0^m=0$. Since $\pi$ is clear exactly when $F(\pi)=\varnothing$,
$$
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if $\pi$ is clear,}\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

**Step 2: sum over all schedules.** Adding this identity over all $n!$ schedules, each clear schedule contributes $1$ and every other schedule contributes $0$:
$$
D_n=\sum_{\pi}\ \sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
$$
This is a sum over pairs $(\pi,S)$ with $S\subseteq F(\pi)$. The condition $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ says that $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ and that $\pi$ fixes every member of $S$. All sums are finite, so we may sum over $S$ first:
$$
D_n=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{|S|}\,\#\{\pi: S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.
$$

**Step 3: count the schedules that fix a given set.** Fix $S$ with $|S|=k$. A schedule with $S\subseteq F(\pi)$ must send each group in $S$ to its own station. Those $k$ stations are then taken, so the other $n-k$ groups must be matched one-to-one with the other $n-k$ stations. Any such matching works, so there are $(n-k)!$ choices, and
$$
\#\{\pi: S\subseteq F(\pi)\}=(n-k)!.
$$
This count does not require the remaining groups to avoid their own stations. A schedule counted here may fix additional labels outside $S$, which is why Step 1 needs the alternating signs to cancel those extra fixed labels.

**Step 4: group the subsets by size.** The count in Step 3 depends only on $k=|S|$, and there are $\binom nk$ subsets of size $k$. Substituting into Step 2 gives
$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk (n-k)!,
$$
which is the first formula. For the second, 
$$
\binom nk(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\,(n-k)!=\frac{n!}{k!},
$$
so
$$
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\frac{n!}{k!}=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Small cases.**

- $n=0$: the only term is $k=0$, giving $D_0=0!/0!=1$. This is the empty schedule.
- $n=1$: $D_1=1!\,(1-1)=0$. The single group must visit the single station, which has the same label.
- $n=2$: $D_2=2!\,(1-1+\tfrac12)=1$. The sole clear schedule is the swap, with group 1 at station 2 and group 2 at station 1.

response:
A box can be perfectly labeled and still have a small surprise waiting inside. This week's surprise was a bundle of blank envelopes, tied with the same string as the correspondence around it. The box had apparently decided that context deserved its own stationery.

We kept the envelopes. Their sizes match several letters in the bundle, and two carry faint impressions where a seal may once have pressed against them. That does not tell us which letter belonged in which envelope. It does give a future reader something to inspect, and it gives us a reason to describe the envelopes alongside the letters rather than treating them as packing material.

The catalogue note now says that the bundle includes eleven blank envelopes. It also records the impressions without identifying them as seals. We can see marks; their cause is less certain. A photograph would help someone decide whether to request the bundle, but the note is useful even before that photograph is made.

This is a small addition to the catalogue. Nobody has uncovered a lost correspondence or solved a mystery. We have simply made the contents a little easier to anticipate. If you request the bundle next week, the envelopes will still be there, kept flat in a separate sleeve within the same box. The string is there too, stored beside them. Some mornings, describing what we kept is most of the story.

For the next visit, we will photograph the strip from the same two marked positions and record grass height at five fixed points. These additions will make the conditions easier to describe. They will not turn an unobserved stem into an observed one. The counts will remain useful as records of what we saw, provided that the change in visibility stays with them when they are summarized.

We found fewer flowering stems on the north slope during the second visit. The count fell from 34 to 19 within the marked strip. We counted stems rather than plants because several plants had more than one stem, and we could not reliably trace them through the ground cover.

The strip was the same on both visits, but the conditions were not. On the first visit, the grass had been recently cut. On the second, it reached above some of the shorter stems. We therefore cannot tell how much of the difference reflects flowering and how much reflects visibility. Keeping the strip fixed controls where we looked; it does not ensure that we saw the same fraction of what was there.

The photographs show three stems that were flowering on the first visit and carried seed heads on the second. Those observations establish that at least some stems had changed stage. They do not account for the whole difference in the counts, and we have not assumed that every stem missing from the second count had set seed.

For the next visit, we will photograph the strip from the same two marked positions and record grass height at five fixed points. These additions will make the conditions easier to describe. They will not turn an unobserved stem into an observed one. The counts will remain useful as records of what we saw, provided that the change in visibility stays with them when they are summarized.
